PROPOSED BAN ON USE OF SODIUM NITRITE IN FOOD PREPARATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that there is irrefutable scientific evidence that sodium nitrite used in the preparation of virtually all cured meats undergoes a chemical change in the meat, after cooking and after ingestion by humans, producing highly carcinogenic chemicals, that the increase in stomach and perhaps other cancers in North America has occurred in direct ratio to the increased use of cured meats containing nitrite and that the supposed safe level of 150 parts per million of nitrite set by the Canadian government is not based on any scientific evidence that this is indeed a safe level, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard):
That the Canadian government take immediate action to ban the use of sodium nitrite in the Canadian food supply, that the government direct its attention to alternative methods of meat preparation and that during the interval until the ban is in complete effect the skull and crossbones or some other appropriate warning be placed on the labels of all foods containing sodium nitrite.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT AGE OF ELIGIBILITY FOR OLD AGE PENSION BE REDUCED TO CREATE JOBS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move an important motion of pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that a large number of young people aged 15 to 24 are unemployed and that a large number of individuals between 60 and 65 years of age are tackling serious problems of survival, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House enjoin the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to take all necessary means in the shortest possible time to introduce in the House a bill whose effect would be to reduce to 60 the eligibility age for old age security pension for persons wishing to retire at that age, which would surely have a considerable impact on the level of unemployment in the country.

speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. It is to the investigation which the Prime Minister is relying on that I should like to direct my question. The Prime Minister is obviously relying on it because it will get at all the involvements, including the government's involvement; at least, that is the case the government would like to put. Is the Prime Minister aware of the effects of the Combines Investigation Act and the power of investigation; that it does not apply where criminal offences may be involved; that there is a limitation on the seizure of documents and the publication of those documents; that the director has no power to order any further inquiry, that that power rests with the government which this inquiry should be investigating? In other words, it is another case of the government investigating itself.
Is the Prime Minister aware that there is no opportunity whatsoever for the public to be informed with respect to the government's involvement? In fact, is the Prime Minister aware that the investigation which he calls for under the Combines Investigation Act is no examination of the government at all, which is the centre point, the keystone, of this cartel which has caused the trouble to Canadian consumers? How can the Prime Minister justify this inquiry, and why does he not have a public inquiry so he can let it all hang out, if his case is so good?

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It is a sincere problem we are facing in response to the Throne Speech delivered a few weeks ago.

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. Malone
Yesterday, just prior to the vote, I was pointing out that in essence what the government has done has been to waste a decade for Canadians. It has wasted our resources, it has wasted our development but, more important still, it has wasted the trust and confidence of Canadians. Take a look at the regional disparities which exist in the country today. We note that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), campaigning in Edmonton in 1974, stated that in no case would rail charges for the short haul exceed those for the long haul. The truth is that the same inequities exist today. Take a look at the abnormalities in freight rate structure categorized by the Department of Transport. In no less that 22 categories anomalies in freight rates continue to exist. Elere we are, three and a half years after the last election, and there are still 22 groups of anomalies in the freight rate structure.
This is the situation to which we have come-one million unemployed, major industries closing down everywhere, not just in the Sudbury basin-small companies overloaded with paperwork. The dollar bills we use today should have been minted rather than printed. We heard last night that for the first time the dollar has dipped into the 80 cent group and the degree of regional disparity is reflected by the fact that the five eastern provinces have 37 per cent of all the unemployed. More despairingly still we find that an added 50 per cent of our young people today are among the unemployed, the unemployment rate having doubled since the present government took office.
Then, there was the startling information that the government will have to contribute some $4 billion in unemployment insurance, up by more than $1 billion as compared with a year ago, which simply illustrates that the government of the day has no strategy for coping with unemployment or satisfying the needs of the nation in terms of providing incentives to develop the economy. The government should be charged with the rape of the nation. In 1968 federal expenditures amounted to $9 billion. Today, those expenditures have risen to $40 billion with a $9 billion deficit. So, when this government took office we had a $9 billion budget and today we have a $9 billion deficit. This shows clearly and succinctly that the government is simply incompetent to run the nation's business. In the six years from 1970 to 1976, federal expenditures increased by 61 per cent. What a waste of the people's money, especially considering that in the same period the consumer price index increased by some 55 points.
In face of all this mismanagement, we have to realize that there has been a double knifing of the farm population of this country. In 1976 we note that farm incomes in Canada increased two per cent but input costs increased 40 per cent. I n other words, farmers had a net drop in income of 38 per cent.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like at this time to move the following motion, seconded by the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That Your Majesty s advisers, by their failure to develop and implement a comprehensive industrial strategy for Canada, are directly responsible for the 
high level of unemployment and the loss of export markets, and have thereby forfeited the confidence of the people of Canada and this House.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many Canadians I was pleased that the Queen, opened this session on the occasion of her Jubilee. I am one of the Canadians who hope Her Majesty will be able to fulfill her royal functions for many years to come with the dignity and graciousness which won her public admiration throughout the world. I also wish to congratulate the two new members who have moved the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Their speeches revealed, of course, their very good knowledge of public affairs and keen awareness of the political situation in Canada. For one of them the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson), whom I had the opportunity to see at work during his electoral campaign, such ability has not come as a surprise to me. He has already held several public offices and is highly qualified to perform his new duties brilliantly as a member of parliament.
The Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, mentioned some of the steps the government intends to take to solve the national unity crisis. Today, I would like to state briefly in what political context these steps should be taken and what results can be expected at this stage of the debate on the Canadian fconfederation.
What progress has been made, in fact, since the Parti Quebecois was elected on November 15, 1976, in Quebec as well as in the other provinces, and at the federal level? In the province of Quebec, as everyone knows, Mr. Levesque's party was elected on the promise to give Quebekers a good government and to postpone the separation of the province until a referendum is held to clarify its mandate. The results of what can be called the electoral trick which brought the Parti Quebecois to power are beginning to show. Quebec is governed by a team of intellectuals and university professors without any experience in government-they are not really conversant with Canada's economic, industrial and technical realities and are in addition, given to dogmatic solutions.
I could give many examples to prove my point, Mr. Speaker, but I will mention only two. The PQ's sudden decision to increase the minimum wage to the highest level in North America stems from a very commendable concern for small wage-earners, but equating the minimum wage with social security while it is in fact an economic measure may well turn out to be more harmful than beneficial for those low income earners themselves.
How many small businesses have been compelled to fire one or two of their half-dozen employees? In fact, if the increase ordered threatens the small and medium size firms which are operating somewhat marginally, and if our competitive position on international markets is adversely affected in such
October 25, 1977

areas as the textile and shoe industries, who will be the first to suffer? Precisely those the government meant to help.
Likewise in the linguistic area. Under the guise of a cultural insecurity which is greatly exaggerated, the Quebec government is likely to complicate more than what would be normally acceptable, among other things the lives of head offices in Montreal. Montreal is admirably situated to serve as a practical link with New York City, where a great many deals are transacted, Toronto, and the rest of Canada. This vocation for Montreal, however, has now been seriously jeopardized. Yet the PQ party would prefer that we did not mention this. It suggests that to show the signs of a sure deterioration of the situation, as evidenced by the shocking number of houses for sale in the City of Montreal, is to indulge in political terror and seek to make a point through fear.
Of course, the economic situation is poor throughout the land, with the possible exception of Alberta where the growth rate is definitely higher than in the rest of the country. Quebec is certainly not the only region to receive hard knocks, but assuming that everything which is taking place in Quebec, that is a decrease in private investment and an unfavourable migratory balance, as it was quite recently pointed out by the new member for Outremont, Mr. Andre Raynauld, assuming that absolutely everything is attributable to the economic situation elsewhere, is it the time then to introduce political changes which are likely to disrupt completely the existing order? Through its propaganda, the PQ would like to generate a liking for Quebec but they themselves do not like Quebecers. They dream of new structures and of building a political authority which will tickle their vanity. They dream of independence when nobody is independent. They preach a state religion while forgetting that of the man they were committed to serve.
One of the things we must denounce in this government is its partisanship, and that is even more frightening than its political options. We have seen that during the great debate on Bill 101. We have been told, among other things, that the Parti Quebecois alone is the embodiment of Quebec's collective soul, that those who do not agree with the party are suspected of sympathizing with Anglophones. But we have seen that the soul of Quebecers is less collective than one would think. When they prevented the distribution of Mr. Keith Spicer's audiovisual kit called "O Canada", a group of citizens of my constituency, of Ahuntsic/Laval-des-Rapides volunteered to distribute these kits to students who asked for them. In my constituency alone, 5,000 kits have been handed out and we ordered 2,000 more to meet the demand. This indicates that Quebecers will never be muzzled, even by a so-called interpretation of their own collective soul.
Likewise when the figures concerning the advantages of Quebec's participation in Confederation were published. What do they do when these figures show something different from what that party would like them to depict? The Quebec government publishes national figures which corroborate its own PQ theory and declares that all those who doubt the official interpretation are incompetent.
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
The main point to be remembered of, Mr. Speaker, is that the PQ team does not feel at ease to govern because of the fundamental ambiguousness of its terms of reference. How can the Levesque government pretend to behave as a good provincial government and work in the interest of Confederation without destroying its own theory to the effect that federalism is a nonsense and Quebec must leave it? There is a fundamental contradiction which even those with the best intentions in the world will eventually be unable to live with.
Good government is not possible so long as the hindrance of independence is not removed. The Parti Quebecois is fooling the people without caring to enlighten them. So many of its statements give rise to confusion: there will be no independence. That is what they said in the beginning; then they said it was inevitable. All of a sudden we were faced with sovereignty-association, as if it were possible to do something and the opposite at the same time. Quebec should at least be honest enough to tell us that sovereignty-association comes necessarily with independence, and then we will see how the people in Quebec will react.
Quebec cooperates with the federal government only when it is a matter of obtaining funds from this government. Nobody is fooled by this ruse. But we, in the federal government, will not refuse that cooperation, even though we do so reluctantly, unwillingly, because we do not want to deprive Quebecers of the benefits of Confederation. As far as we are concerned, Quebec has not yet separated.
What is happening in the rest of the country, because it is also important to know what will be the response of the rest of the country to the present crisis. It seems to me that after the initial shock of November 15, after the kind of disbelief at first in the real intentions of Mr. Levesque and his team, Quebec's partners within the Canadian Confederation are now becoming clear-headed.
Slowly but surely English Canada is realizing that nothing can any longer be as it was before. Right from the outset some provincial premiers expressed a desire to get to the bottom of the problem. There was no outraged denunciation of bill 101, for example, on their part. The provinces, mostly Englishspeaking readily understood that they could not denounce bill 101 introduced by the Quebec government without blaming themselves. Quite fortunately their awareness of that uncomfortable situation prompted them to make the St. Andrews statement which I am sure will soon result in a human and minorities rights charter enshrined in a constitution and solemnly guaranteed by the supreme authority of the law. So we are on the right track.
What did the federal government think at the time bill 101 was introduced? In the name of a pluralistic conception of our society, in the name also of the freedom of movement of citizens throughout the country, in short, in the name of general and noble principles, we could have disallowed bill 101 or challenged its constitutionality before the Supreme Court. Apart from our historical reality and in terms of absolute principles, I for one would be prepared to fight fiercely for the

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
freedom of choice of the language of education in Quebec and in all Canadian provinces.
But is one justified at this particular time in our history to hide behind broad principles when, historically Francophones outside Quebec never obtained from the English provinces, with the exception of Ontario, where a great effort was made, the same rights as the English minority in Quebec?
One may have some feeling today about the situation in Quebec resulting from the passage of Bill 101. Nevertheless, they still enjoy their own public education system. How could we intervene in the name of our power of disallowance when we did not lift as much as a finger when the Francophones of other provinces were the subject of negligence and sometimes of hostility on the part of public authorities? How can one forget the Manitoba law in the beginning of the century when Francophones in that province were deprived of French schools, and the fact that at the time the champions of liberty had not felt that they should fight for those minority rights?
What about the time of this famous rule 17 in Ontario? Where was the federal government with its power of disallowance of that kind of thing? Where was the federal government when 1, as an adolescent student in Ottawa, had to write my examinations in English? To think that today the federal government could have disallowed Bill 101 is to ignore our history.

This is tantamount to ignoring our history and the deep wounds that have not yet healed in the collective unconscious of French Canadians. To denounce the injustice of Quebec towards its English minority in the name of a superior conception of justice that the Anglophones have never respected themselves would have appeared quite indecent to the French Canadians.
When Confederation came into being, the English language then needed protection, since Anglophones were in a minority in Lower Canada. Georges-Etienne Cartier made reference to that when he said: "If we submit to the provincial legislatures and the imperial government a bill to create a general government, it will be our duty to protect equally all ethnic groups and their various interests." The English language was therefore protected in Quebec.
Are we to conclude that as soon as the demographic balance shifted in favour of the Anglophones throughout the country, justice and tolerance were disregarded? Canada was born out of the need for English and French Canadian to work together and it will not survive without this cooperation. The linguistic and cultural issue is not the only one of which Canada as a whole will have to be aware. Already in a minority in Canada as regards language, French Canadians are also dominated economically in their own province. In Montreal for instance, to continue in the same vein of the present debate, the economy is widely controlled by Anglophones and, as some have already said, in a hundred years of existence, none of the

big English banks for instance has ever managed to appoint a French-speaking chairman and executive vice-president. Is it therefore any wonder that French-speaking Canadians are convinced that Anglophones can rise to the top of the economical and political ladder without having to speak French, while a Francophone will never be able to do so unless he is bilingual.
Out of 105 companies operating in Quebec with more than
1,000	employees, 91 are Anglophones. A study of those companies reveals that less than 10 per cent of the executives appointed by their a board of directors are French-speaking. 1 repeat a mere 10 per cent. And 41 of those corporations do not have a single French Canadian at the management level. All this in Quebec! In the face of such facts, it is easily understood why young Quebecers feel frustrated, when they they are relagated to the public service or self-employment, because they have no access to the best jobs available in their province. However, the situation can be corrected. At the federal government level, this is what we have attempted with a large degree of success.
According to a study conducted at my request, federal Crown corporations showed much more encouraging results than the private sector.
Among Crown corporations, the proportion of Frenchspeaking executives is 23 per cent nationally. The proportion is still higher in Quebec, so that province's private sector is clearly lagging behind. Turning to the directorship level, French Canadians account for some 25 per cent of the total number of directors in our Crown corporations.
These statistics would have to be broken down of course to determine whether we are well represented in every area of endeavour of our Crown corporation. I note for instance that at the Canadian Museums Association, the proportion of Francophones is 50 per cent. A brief look at the study shows that we have not last ground in the cultural areas, but on the contrary, we are present in almost every field of endeavour of the federal Crown corporations. This shows that the ratio of French-speaking Canadians at the federal level is in proportion to the French-speaking population and that they have significantly more equal career opportunities.
Perhaps we were warned of such possibility by Sir John A. Macdonald, but the federal government has understood that a sharing of responsibilities was necessary for the harmonious development of the two founding people of our country. 1 quote Sir John A. Macdonald in an admonition to his Englishspeaking fellow-men:
Looking through the directory of civil servants in Lower Canada, you would be surprised to discover your supremacy over all important positions. Be careful that the French people do not discover those facts and do not begin to expose them.
This was written in 1856.
In spite of those mistakes, those oversights and what I would call our lack of faithfulness toward the spirit which led French and English Canadians to tie their destiny, Confederation is not a failure. We are still speaking French, we have developed our identity and we enjoy a standard of living envied by many.
October 25, 1977

Indeed, no province in this country is entirely like the others within that Confederation and each in its own way is demanding changes. All have grievances about Confederation in its present form. For Quebec, of course, this is somewhat more obvious because of the language difference. We have one more grievance to add. However, Saskatchewan, for instance, is under many aspects more different from Ontario than from Quebec. Saskatchewan has the same social democratic concerns as Quebec, for example, and gives the same importance to the cooperative movement which Saskatchewan residents consider to have been an important tool for developing regional culture. In addition, there is in the west the same feeling of alienation which is expressed in various ways according to the events. Moreover, the particularities of the Maritime provinces deserve to be maintained if we want to escape the dullness of uniformization in Canada.
Therefore English Canada itself must become aware of its identity. This identity has many facets. English Canada is not homogeneous. It must decide what characteristics each region wants to safeguard within the unity of Confederation. Some will be discouraged at the idea of assembling such diversities within the Canadian Confederation. For my part, I see in this a source of hope because if it considers itself diversified, English Canada will be better able to understand Quebec aspirations and more stimulated to invent the formulas which would enable everyone to feel Canadian without having to give up his provincial or regional roots.
We must therefore take advantage of the present crisis to rethink our country and to rebuild it with our hands. The real danger is to lose interest in the problem of national unity. Introspection is not easy for individuals and even less so for countries and for entire nations. I have already perceived in some circles in my travels through Ontario a certain weariness about this problem of national unity in areas of Ontario which have been traditionally much closer to us than other provinces. This problem bores people when it does not irritate them.
On this level, it seems to me that the role of the federal government is absolutely crucial. It is up to the central government to spirit up lazy minds so as not to allow the country to slip away from us. Canada can survive only if very many of us want to save it. We are looking for and we must now recall those who want to save the country. Everyone must realize that he has no right to leave this task to his neighbour, because a desire to live together can only exist through individuals who are bent on uniting their destiny and no one can decide for someone else. In that sense the federal government cannot act as a substitute for the English provinces and federalist forces in Quebec to define the details of a new confederative agreement, but it can and it must exercise a leadership such as the Prime Minister has been doing so far.
Taking into consideration the change in mentalities and the new opening in English Canada after the impact of November 15, the Prime Minister did offer to take advantage of this new climate to reopen the constitutional issue and seek a renewed constitution.
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
In the speech he delivered in Quebec City, among others, he just opened doors and some new avenues and he declared himself prepared to join the provinces to launch this great debate. And he committed himself to clean the house from basement to attic if necessary.
But first it was necessary to find out about the tastes and needs of the dwellers of the house, the partitions they wanted to tear down and those they wanted to move away. The Pepin-Robarts Commission has therefore been set up to carry out this inventory and identify on another level the lines of force of any possible evolution or change.
Does this mean that the federal government, now that it has set up thses mechanisms, must sit back and wait? Certainly not, for it would be, in my opinion, a serious mistake on its part. For the federal government has its own message to contribute to this constitutional debate, and it must speak loud and clear. Of course, it is only one of the parties involved in this debate, but the provinces can no more assume its role in the reconstruction effort of our country than it can assume theirs.
It would be easy to re-write the Constitution to please Quebec, or to re-write it to please English Canada. But the real challenge is the one which is confronting us now, that of finding a formula which would be universally practical, without necessarily boxing up the country in a carcan which would render it powerless when faced with diverging regional interests. And the super-challenge is that of defining that new balance between the centre and the areas without the active and interested co-operation of the PQ government now in power. The participation of the Quebec people will definitely be needed because the government itself will not co-operate in that endeavour.
It therefore seems that, in coming months, people will have to remember first that any federal offer to the provinces can only be partial since it comes from the central government. The new constitution cannot be brought forth by the federal government as if by magic. And even if, fortunately, we did discover the magic formula, it would still have to be rediscovered and reinvented jointly with the provinces.
On the other hand, the people can rightly expect us to be imaginative in the invention of new ways in which to exercise powers at both the federal and provincial levels. 1 feel that Canadians are justified in asking their central government to develop institutional changes to help us go from a federalism of confrontation to a federalism of "concertation".
Whatever new spirit we may hope will come from a new constitution, the fact still remains that in the meantime, and even after, any measure taken by the Canadian government shall, as I said earlier, take into account the past and the common subconsciousness of both founding groups. As Georges-Etienne Cartier once said "in trusting a federal government, the French-speaking population is showing confidence in our English-speaking compatriots. Would it be asking too much of the English that they trust the liberalism and the fair-mindedness of the French in local government?"

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to say what a pleasure it was for me to hear the Speech from the Throne read by Her Majesty in the other place and to have an opportunity of seeing her at the various functions in Ottawa, as well as for my wife and me to meet Her Majesty and His Royal Highness Prince Phillip at the reception here in the parliament buildings. I should like also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
If it would not be considered irreverent by the House, I should like to say that recent actions of the government remind me of a story told me by Howard Clark, the former Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada. The story concerned a little girl who had a sports day coming on a certain Saturday so she was hoping for good weather. She believed in God and so she prayed all week for good weather. She was disappointed, however, because it rained on the Saturday and the sports day was not a great success. Her father was not a believer. He thought it nonsense to believe in a Supreme Being and he said to his daughter, "You see, your prayers were not answered because it is raining today." The little girl showed her faith by replying, "Oh no Daddy, God answers. He always answers. It is just that today the answer was no."
I was reminded of that story because I know that Canadians have been praying the government would take some action to get this country moving again, to get people working again, to cure the many ailments of the country. I am sure that Canadians praying for action must have felt as the little girl did, that God-in this case the government-had said there were not going to be any goodies that particular day.
I want to mention two areas of the Speech from the Throne that may seem unrelated, Mr. Speaker, but I can assure the House that I shall relate them to one another. One is dividends on stocks of Canadian companies and the other is unemployment insurance. The connection may seem tenuous but I hope you will not feel that way when I have finished my remarks.

Let me begin by referring to the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). The document we were handed that day looked very much like the budget document handed to us on March 31 and I thought we were getting a budget or a mini-budget. The government insists it was neither but simply an economic and fiscal statement. Whatever it is called, Mr. Speaker, it made only passing mention of unemployment and unemployment insurance. I thought that odd because in the Speech from the Throne Her Majesty made some moving comments about unemployment, unemployment insurance, inflation and ail the other problems we face in Canada today. I should like to read a couple of sentences. At one point Her Majesty said:
High rates of unemployment and inflation are clear signals of the inadequacy of economic strategies appropriate to simpler times.
That may be the case, but I wonder if it should not have made reference to simpler minds rather than simpler times. We must ask ourselves who has been in power for the last 14 years? Who has been in charge of the affairs of this country? Fourteen years is long enough to make any changes considered desirable.
Perhaps Her Majesty's remarks concerning unemployment in Canada were more moving when she said:
The human hardship imposed by the current level of unemployment in Canada is deeply disturbing. It is neither just nor tolerable that in this country there should be so many men and women deprived of the dignity of self-supporting work, unable to meet their financial commitments and plan confidently for the future. It is intolerable that so many are deprived of their right to secure and productive lives, and that their families bear an unfair burden of worry, uncertainty, and deprivation.
Those are very moving words and describe quite accurately,
I am sure, the problems and feelings of many Canadians who find themselves in that position through no fault of their own. It seems strange that the government has repeatedly refused to adopt a solution suggested by this side of the House which I am certain would have positive effects on the economic condition of the country and be effective in relieving unemployment. The government says that, of course, all these policies are not going to work, that they are on trial, unproven. The answer to that is that the policies the government has applied have been tried and proven not to work.
The Minister of Finance said that dividends will remain under control for at least another six months, until April 1978 and the increase will be restricted to 6 per cent instead of the 8 per cent allowed previously. Some two years ago in the AntiInflation Act then before this House there was a provision that dividends would be frozen, that no increase would be allowed. That provision ignored the fact that many Canadians had taken action to provide for their own wellbeing in old age and relied to a large extent on dividends from investments made from their savings.
The government eventually realized it would be unfair to allow wages to increase by up to 12 per cent while freezing dividends at the level of the year before even though inflation continued. Now, we find they have taken a similar step in principle and restricted the amount of increase on dividends to 6 per cent all the while admitting that inflation will be in
October 25, 1977

excess of 8 per cent. The numbers may be a little different but the principle is the same. The government has ignored the fact that the provisions now put forth are imposing a hardship on those very people who have been thrifty and saved and now rely on dividends for a portion of their income. It is cruel to allow inflation to continue at 8 per cent while restricting dividends which form part of a person's income to 6 per cent.
1 see it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I shall continue my remarks at two o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, before the lunch hour I was commenting on the policy of the government in restricting dividends, a practice which inflicts a penalty upon retired Canadians who rely on dividends for a portion of their income. The government may say, "Yes, but we have indexed pensions to protect the retired people of this country". However, I think we should note that probably only one-third of the workers currently in Canada are covered by any kind of retirement pension plan besides the government pension plan, which provides at best a limited benefit. Of course, private pension schemes are not indexed, and retired people are therefore left on their own to get their income out of their savings.
I think the most important aspect, however, of the freeze on dividends-and the biggest negative factor-is the effect that it has on investment in Canada. Capital, as well as labour, is hit. Capital, naturally, cannot be invested at low rates while there is a high rate of inflation, so if we have a rate of inflation of 8 per cent, capital has to seek the real return that it earns in addition to the 8 per cent. That is why mortgage rates in Canada today exceed 12 per cent. In its search for high returns, capital is discouraged, therefore, from investing in Canada because of the freeze on dividends, or at least the limitation to a 6 per cent increase. If there is no investment of capital in Canada, there will be no creation of new jobs.
Workers all over Canada who have their savings held in pension funds are also interested in the dividend rate because the accumulated dividends in pension funds all over Canada become investment capital for the future, thus creating jobs. When dividends are restricted and capital formation, therefore, is restricted as well, those jobs will not be available. Capital probably finds its best investments in other areas where regulations are not so strict.
The Address-Mr. B. Clarke
I think I have arrived at the tie-in between dividends and unemployment insurance. As I said at the beginning, I want to talk about dividends and unemployment insurance and 1 will tie the two subjects together. Many members may not realize how important a topic unemployment insurance is. It would be well to remind the House that the estimated current expenditures on unemployment insurance-that is, payments to those unemployed-in the current fiscal year is estimated to be $4,200 million, over $4 billion. In order to get that figure in proper perspective, I remind the House that it is approximately 10 per cent of the total budgetary estimates of the government of Canada for this fiscal year.
Another way of relating it to the over-all financial situation is that unemployment insurance payments will approximate one half of the total budgetary deficit for the current fiscal year. It is now projected to be over $9 billion. Therefore, we are talking about an expenditure, in total, of over $4.2 billion. That is a large enough expenditure. However, the problem of unemployment insurance is two-sided. Not only do the unemployed add to the expenditures of Canada, but because they are not employed, they are not earning wages and, therefore they are not paying taxes and not adding to the revenues of Canada. Therefore, there is a double loss to the country. On the one hand, we have people taking money from the treasury; at the same time, those people are not in a position to put money into the treasury. 1 am in no way suggesting that it is their fault; I suggest it is the fault of the policies of the government opposite.
The government will boast of all the new jobs that are created. What they do not tell us when boasting of their
200.000	new jobs, is that the number of workers exceeded the number of new jobs created in this past year by some 128,000. There are 128,000 people coming into the work force where no jobs exist. Until they have a job in the work force, there are no unemployment insurance benefits because they have not worked to earn the credits that are necessary.
The minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) both announced a new program of $150 million to develop some
30.000	temporary jobs. It is worth comparing that with the total problem. At today's rate of unemployment insurance, the $150 million will keep the unemployed in benefits for a little over one week. This is hardly a program one can laud on the basis it will take care of the problems. It is a lot like many other government give-aways that we have seen in the past, give-aways which may attract a little favour in the government's direction but which really do nothing in the way of creating permanent jobs that Canadians want today.
For some five years I have campaigned against this kind of government give-away. 1 started with the Local Initiatives Program and Opportunities for Youth. Certainly, the recipients of these programs were enamoured by the fact that they were getting a few dollars. However, when you sat them down and pointed out that at the end of that particular program they would be back on the sidewalk without a job, they could see it was just a trick of the government to take the heat off.

We now have the spectacle of Canada Works. 1 do not know how it is working in all parts of the country, but the figures in my constituency may be typical. In Vancouver Quadra we had applications for Canada Works grants totalling $1.2 million. The budget for Vancouver Quadra was $100,000. The government has funded less than 10 per cent of the need. If there are members opposite who think Vancouver Quadra should be entitled to more, I will agree with them.
Even the Liberal government would have difficulty in justifying how nine constituencies in British Columbia received the minimum of $100,000, while two Liberal constituencies-one of the minister from Skeena-received $4'/2 million, and the other, Coast Chilcotin, received over $2 million. One would not want to suggest there is anything political about those allegations, but one might have to guess at it. The government recognized that there may be a need, and they designed a program. The shortfall is alarming. In the case of the unemployed and the $150 million, one week of benefits is covered by this little extra gift. In the case of Canada Works, less than 10 per cent of the need in my area was met by such a program.
We on this side of the House, my leader in particular, have called for a major overhaul of unemployment insurance payments. First, the government has to decide whether unemployment insurance is to be an insurance scheme or a welfare scheme. At the moment it is hard to see any difference between unemployment insurance paid as a kind of welfare item, and other give-aways which the government brings in from time to time. It would be easy for the government to let Canadians know the cost of their unemployment insurance plan. At the moment it does not matter about the level of unemployment; the government picks up the tab for the shortfall between the payments out and payments in by workers and employers. This year the shortfall will be something like $1.7 billion. I am not sure Canadian taxpayers really care whether they pay that kind of cost through tax premiums or through tax payments into general revenue. However, it is only fair of the government to let Canadians know the cost of this kind of program.
When talking about costs you need to take a much closer look at unemployment insurance abuses. Here we have not just the attack on individuals who may be abusing the system, and that certainly exists. We have all heard of the Canadian ski team at Banff getting their cheques mailed to them, and the thousands of cheques that went unclaimed during the last postal strike because whoever the unemployed were, they were not interested or needy enough to pick up their cheques when they were made available to them.
It is not only individual abuses: there are abuses of the system by the system. That is the kind of abuse which allows high income earners to collect unemployment insurance during the off season. I know one fisherman on the west coast who can earn $60,000 during the season, and quite legally collect unemployment insurance in the off season. He is perfectly entitled to that because that is the way the rules are. We on

this side happen to think that unemployment insurance was not intended for that kind of individual.
We do not intend to lose sight of the regional disparities in Canada. We know very well there are areas on the Atlantic coast, for example, where job openings are non-existent and the number of people seeking work is enormous. We also know there are people in other areas in a similar situation. If I may use the example of Edmonton, there are people unemployed although there are many jobs going begging. In those cases, people would rather be unemployed than go to work.
We can trace that attitude back to the government policy which has made it attractive to be on unemployment insurance. There is certainly a need for real protection. We are not in any way suggesting that the breadwinner of the family who is genuinely unemployed should in any way lose the protection of the unemployment insurance scheme. However, we are not at all certain that Canadians, recipients or payers, want it to be a welfare scheme, which is the way it seems to be right now. We see that the policies of this government have created practically a whole generation of people who have no incentive to work, because the government has made it so attractive not to work. We think the system needs an overhaul so that kind of situation can no longer exist.
I said I would relate these two apparently unrelated topics. I hope I have made it clear how they are related. I think they need to be considered together. We urge the government to come up with some kind of comprehensive economic plan which will get Canada moving. We do not need so-called economic and fiscal statements of the kind the minister gave us last week to tell us what the government hopes to do by way of piecemeal efforts. What is needed is a comprehensive plan which would solve a few of these problems all at once, instead of all these stop-gap measures we are getting from the government.

The minister says she is resisting this pressure. Mr. Speaker, it appears to me she is going to need some strength if that resistance is to be effective. Then, of course, she comes out with the old saying that this is a period in which we have to exercise restraint, in which we have to save money, and maybe it is in the field of our social programs that this restraint will have to be shown. Mr. Speaker, that is utter nonsense. Furthermore, it is cruel and heartless.
The government is in trouble, there is no doubt about that. But there is no reason why a government which finds itself in trouble, particularly in the economic field, should look first of all to its workers and the wages they get and, along with workers, at our old age pensioners and other recipients of various social security benefits and say that those programs have to be cut back.
It is precisely because there is uncertainty in this country and precisely because of a lack of confidence in our future that this is the time, I suggest, when we should be eliminating causes of unfairness and moving faster in the direction of fairness and equality for our people. If we tell our older citizens and our veterans that they are the ones who must make sacrifices in the interest of a government which is in trouble we shall not add to confidence in this country but, rather, we shall lessen it. 1 therefore suggest once again that not only should cut backs be avoided but that there should be advances in our social legislation.
Before anyone asks me whether we can afford it, or where the money is coming from, I would ask the House once again to look at this whole matter in its proper perspective. What has to be considered is not just the figures in the budgets of our various governments but the total production of Canada and the extent to which we are letting our older people share in that production. The estimates for the year show that Ottawa is spending about $5 billion toward the provision of old age security, guaranteed income supplements and other means of maintaining the incomes and the lives of our older people.
I do not know how much other income Canadians 65 years of age and over receive and 1 doubt whether it is possible to put this information together from the statistics available. But I do know some things. 1 know that 30 per cent of the nearly two million Canadians who are over 65 have nothing else but their old age security and their guaranteed income supplement upon which to live. 1 know, also, that a further 30 per cent of those 65 and over have very little else because they qualify for part of the income supplement. I know that many others in the
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
top 40 per cent are experiencing difficulty in getting by in these times of inflation. Therefore 1 think I am doing a bit of legitimate and justified guessing when l say 1 doubt whether the total income in the hands of our senior citizens is more than about $8 billion, $5 billion of which comes out of the federal treasury and the rest from some of the provincial treasuries as well as from incomes which some of those over 65 might receive from other sources. My figure could be wrong. Maybe it is too high. If it is too low, I am sure the total does not go beyond $9 billion or $10 billion. But 1 believe I am pretty close to the truth when 1 suggest the figure is about $8 billion-I am talking about the total income of the two million Canadians who are aged 65 or over.
These people represent about one-twelfth of the population. But if that one-twelfth is receiving only $8 billion of income each year I ask our members to relate that figure to our gross national product-not to the budgets of governments, but to what we produce in this country. What does our gross national product-gross national expenditure as Statistics Canada calls it-amount to in a year? It is running in excess of $200 billion. The $8 billion which we provide for our senior citizens is one twenty-fifth of the total production of this country. That is, we are giving one twenty-fifth of the total production of this country to one-twelfth of the people. That is mean, inhumane and unfair, and hon. members, whether in the cabinet or elsewhere, have no right to suggest that this is a time to cut back on social programs, that this is a time to cut back on old age security or, indeed, on family allowances, although that is another matter which is separate from the statistics that I have been giving.

process. But they built this country to the point where it can now produce that much wealth in the course of a year. This is why 1 call for an increase in the basic amount of old age security. Any government that cannot direct the affairs of this country so that a group of people as large as the senior citizens are do not get their share is a government that does not deserve to sit across the way.
Not only do 1 call for an increase in the basic amount of old age security; I call for the escalation formula to be reviewed and put on a proper basis. It is good that there is escalation, that the pension moves up a little bit every three months. But it is always behind. It always relates to the increase in the cost of living which took place several months ago as compared with a few months earlier still. It is never an increase to enable senior citizens to meet the cost increases of the current month or quarter. So I call for a review of the whole escalation formula.
1 also call for a lowering of the eligible age, certainly for those who are out of the labour market. 1 am not at the point of saying that there should be universal pensions at the age of 60 in the way we have them at 65, but 1 am saying that all those who are out of, or are prepared to leave, the labour market and who are between the age of 60 and 65 should have the right to their old age security at that time.
This leads me to say that I agree with the hundreds of persons, especially women, who write in because they find it incredible that a couple of years ago this parliament passed a piece of legislation having to do with spouse's allowance, providing a payment to a spouse, man or woman, between the age of 60 and 65 so long as that spouse is married to and living with an older pensioner, yet which provides nothing at all for the person of single status, widow, spinster, widower or bachelor. In most cases, those who are denied pensions in this category are spinsters or widows. But those who write to me just do not believe this. They write, "Mr. Knowles, did parliament pass that?" They do not believe that the parliament of a civilized country would have been so uncivilized. I call for this spouse's allowance to be replaced by an old age security pension which is available to everyone between the age 60 and 65 who is out of the labour market.
I also call, Mr. Speaker, for amendments to be made to the Canada Pension Plan. There are a number of technical improvements that I should like to deal with, but they can be

raised, at some other time. I want to make once more the main point which was made this morning by one of my hon. friends to my left in a motion under Standing Order 43, namely, that we should lower the eligible age under the Canada Pension Plan to 60 for those who leave the labour market.
I know there is a lot of talk about the right of people to work until they are 65 or 70, or 85 or 90 as some of us might like to do. But the fact is that many workers, especially those in the heavy and dirty industries, can hardly stand the racket until they are 65. If you gave them the chance to retire at 60 on old age security and on the Canada Pension Plan, as well as on any other pension they might have, you would immediately release from the labour market many thousands. This would be of help in alleviating the unemployment situation at the present time. Why keep these older people working with their noses to the grindstone, when they would be entitled to pensions and there are younger people who want the jobs? These are reforms that must be made, and I call on the government to make them in this session of parliament, despite all this talk about restraint and there not being any money to spend on social programs.
I also plead for a new look to be taken at what we are doing for our handicapped people. We have been slow in getting anywhere in this area. The Canadian Council on Social Development a few weeks ago published a very thick volume on the state of our programs for the handicapped of this country. That volume tells a story of a hit and miss operation which does not really recognize the fact that a decent, humane society would try to put those who have handicaps in a position as nearly equal as possible to others. This runs all the way from the structural changes which we should make in our buildings, to special equipment, wheelchairs, transportation, hearing aids and all the rest of it, including adequate pensions or allowances for the blind, to whom we owe a special responsibility. These matters we have hardly touched. We have made a start and we have some legislation, but we are not going to be able to call ourselves a decent, civilized society until these people get all they really need in order to live life as nearly as possible on the basis that it is lived by those whose health and physical capacities are good.
So, Mr. Speaker, I plead for more attention to be paid to the blind and the disabled. Let us not have any talk about this not being the kind of session when these things can be done. It is precisely because there is unhappiness in Canada, because there is a feeling that things are not fair, that we should correct the situation my moving in this direction.
I turn now to another question which I think should be dealt with in this parliament, and that is the whole question of the escalating or indexing of pensions. I know there are certain spokesmen for insurance companies and other bodies who are carrying on campaigns against the indexing of the pensions of public servants, retired RCMP, armed forces personnel, and so on. They argue, why should these people have their pensions indexed when other Canadians do not? That is a good point; if some get it, others should. But the answer to that question is not to take away escalation from those to whom we have given
October 25, 1977

it; rather, let us make it the law that every pension should escalate. Every pension should be indexed. A pension which does not keep up with at least the rising cost of living-and in my view it should keep up with the rising standard of living- is not a pension at all.
These people who are spending money complaining about such indexing as there is should spend their money, their energy and their thought in going in for the proper indexing of all pensions, requiring private pension plans to be indexed or setting up a government scheme for it. In that way things would be a lot better. 1 know there are those who like to say, "What will it cost down the years? Will future generations be able to afford the pension plans that we build up?" I have said it many times, but let me say it again.

speechtext: Say it again, Stanley.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you. My good friend always encourages me to keep going. People on pensions do not live on savings. They do not live on food, clothing and shelter which they have saved from the days when they worked. They live on current production. They live on a portion of what society is producing today. Pensions are just a form of bookkeeping. Just as we decide that children, even though they do not work, will be cared for, so we decided by the granting of pensions that older people will get their share of the wealth that is being produced by a society which is more productive and more capable because they brought it to that point.
This being the reality of the situation, we should start with the simple proposition that retired people should get a pension to enable them to continue to enjoy life as they enjoyed it at the point of retirement, and that they should be able to keep up with the rising cost of living. 1 go further by saying that 1 should like to see the day when pensions will rise in accordance with the rising standard of living. At least, if we can get it across the board that pensions must keep up with the rising cost of living, that will be a real improvement.
1 hope the studies being made under the direction of the government, under the direction of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare will come up with something very soon. I hope those studies will answer this nonsense that we have had against the escalation of pensions. Instead of allowing that nonsense to continue, I hope we will start attacking the real problem, which is to see to it that the pensions of all our people are properly indexed.
My friend who spoke before me had a bit to say about pensions. He talked about them in another context, but he made the point that very few Canadians who retire have a private pension plan at all. Of course, that just shows that what we really need today is to enlarge greatly the scope of the Canada Pension Plan. 1 hope the day will come when the Canada Pension Plan will be large enough and the percentage of one's earnings while he was working, that he receives as a
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
pension, will be large enough so that our older people will really have a break in being able to live on their combined old age security and Canada Pension Plan.
Mr. Speaker, that almost leads me to the remarks 1 had in mind by way of summing up this little speech, but I will save what I had in mind to the end because there are a couple of other things I still want to say. First, I mention once again the railway pensions. It is good that there have been some increases. Even the CPR finally got around to the point of making a slight increase in the pensions of those who retired some years ago. 1 have been receiving interesting mail on this point. 1 get letters from some who are delighted. An extra $20 or $30 a month to a retired person who is just getting by seems a good deal, and they are most grateful for the efforts which have been made on their behalf.
1 get letters from others who get a small amount or who are left out altogether, and they wonder how long the CPR is going to get away with it. Both the CPR and CNR should be required by law, by this parliament and by this government, to excalate the pensions of their retired workers and the survisors of those workers, in accordance with the rising cost of living.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am proud of what this parliament has done. I am proud of what my generation has done. My generation has been in this battle, in politics, in the church, in trade union movements, in farm organizations, and what have you, for 40 or 50 years. I am proud of what we have done in bringing forward these social programs. But unless we extend them, unless we cover everyone, and unless we escalate them to keep up with the rising cost of living, their value will deteriorate and instead of having a happy, contented and satisfied generation of older Canadians we will have people who will be complaining, as everyone else does, about a government which does not know how to run this country.
Before my time runs out, I should like to say a few words about another group, and I refer to our veterans. I am glad to see that my good friend, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), is with us this afternoon. We all have a great deal of respect for him. For myself, I appreciate and welcome the way 1 feel he fights with those cabinet colleagues of his for the break our veterans ought to get.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
