speechtext: Not hard enough.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes. the interjection by my friend, the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), is quite correct. It is not hard enough, but he is fighting as hard as he can. But with the colleagues he has, he has to fight a lot harder.
Just as I am disappointed that there was no reference to old age security in the Speech from the Throne which Her Majesty read to us, so was I deeply disappointed that the Minister of Veterans Affairs was not able to get into that speech some reference to veterans. I pleaded with him during the last session to try to get the cabinet to agree to that, but there was

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
no reference in it at all. Well, that means we do not have a guarantee that anything will be done in this session for veterans. The fact that we do not have the guarantee does not mean we cannot persuade the minister to do something.
The first thing I should like to talk about is the wide gap which has developed between the average wage paid to five designated categories of public servants and the basic rate of the 100 per cent disability pension. As the minister knows, four or five years ago we passed legislation making the 100 per cent pension equal to the average income of five designated groups in the public service. That is where it started 50 or 55 years ago. We got away from it, but we got it back again three or four years ago. Already, it is out of line again. Now there is a gap of over $500 a year between that average which we accepted as a goal and the amount that veterans on the 100 per cent disability pension are receiving. Of course, if there is that gap with regard to the 100 per cent pension, it runs all down the line.
One thing veterans' organizations are pleading for most is the closing of that gap. Let us not wait another 20, 30 or 40 years until we get it back there again. Let us do it now. 1 plead with the minister to get that through his cabinet in this session of parliament.
Also, I plead with him on behalf of the widows of veterans, particularly those whose husbands' disability pensions were less than 48 per cent. For those cases there are no pensions at all. There is a lot which is good about our veterans' legislation, but to say to a widow, "If your husband had 48 per cent or more, you get the full pension; but if your husband's maximum was 47 per cent or less, you get nothing" is just about as inhuman and cruel as it can be. In these days, the number of widows who are being left with no pension at all is increasing. This is of concern to the veterans. 1 hope the minister will get action on that in this session. He must!
Also, I hope he will do something about a very small group of Canadian veterans-200 or fewer-who are survivors of World War I, who were prisoners of war in that first conflict and who were not covered. It is not our fault, nor the fault of the committee. It is not the fault of the minister. It was the fault of his cabinet colleagues that they were not covered in the legislation providing for prisoners of war compensation. It would cost only a small amount of money for those 200 people in the years they have left to live. They are all in their eighties or higher. Surely that is something this parliament can do.
While he is at it, perhaps the minister can also do something about the prisoners of war compensation for the escapers and evaders who were not actually taken prisoners but lived a very precarious existence on the continent of Europe in the last war.
I have no hesitation in saying that there is a lot that is good about our veterans' legislation, but that does not relieve us from the responsibility of improving it in such areas as those I have mentioned. The same goes for the War Veterans Allowance Act; there is a lot that is good about it. I am glad a

review is taking place, and I hope that review will come up with something that is good for our veterans.
I see that the clock is getting around to the point where you will move to the edge of your chair, Mr. Speaker, so perhaps I better wind up. I am always glad, as I say, to have the chance in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne to speak on a subject 1 have spoken about in the House, I suppose, a thousand times. That is not an exaggeration if you multiply the number of times per year I have spoken on it, by the number of years I have been here. I am proud of what we have done from the days when the pension was $20 a month at age 70, with a means test. I am proud of all the things that have been added, and I am proud of the improvements we have made for railway workers, retired civil servants, RCMP, armed forces and veterans.
But, sir, this is a different age from the one in which we started these campaigns. It is an age when we are producing $200 billion of goods and services in this country, and we have no right to stand and boast of what we have done in the last 40 or 50 years unless we give these people their rightful place in sharing what we now produce.
So 1 plead most strongly that these matters be dealt with in this session of parliament. 1 call in particular on the Minister of Health and Welfare and on the Minister of Veterans Affairs to do the job that is theirs in cabinet. If they do that, we can be proud of what we have done in this session of parliament to make life better for our senior Canadians and for our veterans. In doing so, we can make Canada a country of which all of us can be justly proud.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me first to congratulate very sincerely the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) for having been asked to move the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. As could be expected, he agreed with the contents of the throne speech and this is due to the strict discipline of the majority party. Congratulations also to the seconder of the motion. It must be recognized that both members discharged their duty in a truly graceful manner. I acknowledge in spite of my short experience in this House that those two members should be very sincerely congratulated and this is what I am doing.
1 am pleased to sit in this House, Mr. Speaker, on account of the mutually granted respect despite our differences of opinions and principles applying to the administration of the country. I think that the Canadian Parliament is an example for every democracy. It is really fantastic to note how members readily comply with the procedure while suggesting at times some corrections to try to improve it further. That is what democracy is all about and we must try to defend and improve it.
The Speech from the Throne is certainly the best listing of good intentions 1 have ever heard. Statements on the deplorable economic situation, on the catastrophic rate of unemployment and on our fragile national unity are to the point. Indeed we have been saying so for quite a long time. They are not new


October 25, 1977

realities and too many Canadians have lived with them too long. The throne speech points out the urgency of radically revamping Canada's economy. Finally, we have come to realize that something has to be done.
Now if we decide not to wait a hundred years to do something, 1 think we will succeed in demonstrating that Canada is not only a prosperous country but a country which considers its riches and does whatever is required to ensure their distribution to provide Canadians with a fair standard of living. Nothing is more obvious and that is exactly what the Social Credit Party of Canada has been claiming all along. I repeat that pious intentions and band-aid measures will never put the country back on the right track. What is needed is nothing less than a sound and intelligent reorganization of Canadian economic and monetary structures.
Mr. Speaker, the government is not proposing any concrete measures. For instance, the Speech deals with the new funding proposals which were made recently to the provinces in the area of social services. Two sentences further, it reads, and 1 quote:
It is hoped that the response of provincial governments will lead to the introduction .. .
-and realization. We had better hope indeed, when we consider the great constitutional problem which stands in the way of these projects and the bargaining we have to go through. Let us hope. What is needed is not only hope, but action. Why not give the provinces the fiscal jurisdiction they need to administer their services without their having to beg the federal government for money over and over again? The services would be more efficient, for they would be adapted to local requirements and that is why, as members of the Social Credit Party of Canada, at our last convention last weekend we adopted a constitutional position in keeping with the intention our Founding Fathers had when the first four Canadian provinces met and decided to establish the Canadian Confederation.
Then the federal government is a creature of the provinces and, if we want them to be able to carry out their responsibilities to the people of Canada, we must provide them with the necessary revenues to fulfil their financial obligations, and this is the reason why we definitely support the principle of a new constitution, tailored to Canadian conditions and drafted by the provinces, in which the jurisdictions of the central government and the provinces will be clearly set out. I think this is the only way we can ever hope to live together in harmony in this country.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, what each of us is trying to achieve is peace, security and freedom. That is what we are seeking, whether we are French speaking, English speaking or new Canadians, we all want peace, security and freedom. That is why we all have to work together to determine the areas of provincial and federal jurisdictions. They should be clearly defined. We should have enough brains to do that, otherwise there is no point in having all those universities, political scientists, academics, economists and what not, if we are not able to come out with a sensible solution which will be
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
acceptable to the whole country. This is our position with regard to the constitution, Mr. Speaker: respect of all by all and also respect for such covenant, such constitution as we shall choose to give ourselves.
Last July, during the debate on the motion of the Prime Minister, I explained in the House how we intend to meet to prepare this new constitution. 1 shall now repeat it. It may not be the only possible way, but it comes from the heart of a sincere Canadian who loves his country and who would like to preserve it under its present name, in its present dimension, but in such a way that we shall all be happy to live in this country instead of tearing at each other. We must work together to give to our children a country with a constitution that meets our aspirations and which is in complete accordance with the thoughts of the Fathers of Confederation.
We suggest that the provinces designate representatives outside of politics for a meeting that will take as long as it has to and that the federal government also designate someone outside politics, with representatives from the intermediate classes, from chambers of commerce, from finance, from industry, from national associations, from all organizations which have an interest in this country, and that those people, in accordance with the representations that they have been making for many years, develop a constitution project which will then be submitted to the attention of the provinces who can then decide among themselves if this constitution formula is appropriate. If they decide that it is, after defining the role of the federal government, they will invite representatives from the national and provincial political levels and then determine if the formula which has been studied and developed is valid. If such is the case, then comes the matter of the referendum. Mr. Speaker, our party was the first to suggest the idea that questions as important as this one should be submitted to the population through a referendum.
As secretary treasurer for many years, I have been somewhat involved in the question of referendums. This is where we must be careful.
The wording of the question might distort completely the aim of the referendum. That is what matters. The question should be plain. The question should be put in objective and clear terms so that when the woman, the old man, the worker or the farmer go to the poll to cast their vote they understand perfectly the question put to them, or that when they vote by "yes" or "no", their vote not be negative but positive. That is what matters, Mr. Speaker.
The Speech from the Throne details the efforts made under youth employment programs, but it fails to mention that the government spends a lot more on unemployment insurance than on those programs. I do not believe that that is an enticement to work. As for the supporting measures allowing the private sector to undertake projects in other countries, I cannot help but call them scandalous.
If we see fit to channel Canadian money into great projects in other countries, we should have enough courage to do the

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
same in our own country. If such initiatives are likely to create jobs elsewhere, we are likely to create jobs in our country if we do the same here. I think we should help underdeveloped countries but let us not allow our economy in Canada to decline at the same time pretexting that we have no money to help.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I admit that I am a little disappointed to see that the government does not make any mention of the high unemployment levels with the hope that the situation will improve. On the contrary, we are told that the high unemployment and inflation rates demonstrate clearly that the economic methods of an often complex period are no longer applicable. It took the government many years to become aware of this.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is a bit thick. Major Douglas and other enlightened economists have advised governments for years that the present capitalist economic system, and I do not use the word capitalist in a derogatory manner, is ill and that it is in dire need of remedies. That has been going on for years and still nobody does anything. Band-aid measures are taken, governments try to patch things up as best as they can but a new formula is neither accepted nor applied.
Mr. Speaker, will the government at last, and they themselves admitted to this failure, introduce a minimum yearly guaranteed income plan? I put the question yesterday to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and she gave me an affirmative answer. But will it come about soon? Such a measure, combined with a retail discount for Canadian products, would only increase productivity because the national effort would be rewarded.
In addition, the purchasing power thus increased in turn can only lead to better productivity. Mr. Speaker, in this regard I was surprised to read in the newspaper Le Devoir for October 24 a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). The article is entitled, and I quote:
Canadians Save To a Fault
I am absolutely flabbergasted, Mr. Speaker. The government, through its Minister of Finance, advises the people they will have to tighten their belts, that the government will have to spend less. Yet, that same Minister of Finance tells us two days later that Canadians save too much.
I therefore would like to quote a few lines from that editorial:
According to the Minister of Finance, Canadians who do not produce enough, save to a fault.
In every class of society, he said, but more specifically in the middle classes, expenses do not grow in proportion to increased incomes.
Canadians, he feels, "demand a lot but do not necessarily spend. They merely want to save for the future".
But, Mr. Speaker, what does saving for the future mean? It means that they no longer have confidence in the Canadian economy, that they are worried about tomorrow, that is all. And, on the other hand, can we blame them? Thrift is a virtue!

Commander Desjardins, the founder of Credit Unions, taught us this virtue when he founded this economy inspired movement with a view to bringing children and adults to save their pennies and dollars, so that together we may be in a position to build and develop a business or an industry, within our community and give young people the opportunity to save money for their future. I belong to this generation, Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who still believe in thriftiness. But we should not let this seven headed monster that we call inflation harm us and get away with it.
Inflation, as we know it today, is bringing Canadian economy to its knees, it is tolling the knell of private enterprise. All we see about us are bankruptcies. Industries produce less, close their doors, lay-off their employees. In short, inflation creates misery. Inflation breeds unemployment. Inflation plays havoc with the savings of people who have worked on small wages for 40 or 50 years and tried to put a little money aside for their old age. Today, these people have to spend their scant savings on overpriced commodities. The consequence of that is to further diminish the small wages they used to make and the small savings they may have set aside. Yet there is something worse than that and this is why it must be said and we have to tackle this dreadful problem: the case of the Young People. What is going to happen to them? Young couples who buy a house at today's inflationary prices and who will be bound for the next 30 or 40 years to meet their obligations based on today's wages. This situation cannot last or otherwise it is of no use to have experience.
We know for a fact that someday we will have a recession. We are aware of the fact that incomes will be drastically reduced therefore these people who commit themselves today to meet certain obligations in order to acquire a home will necessarily have to give up the hope of ever keeping it. Their creditor will demand payment of the mortgage they signed and as these people will not be able to meet their obligations they will have to give up their home and then the mortgagee will be able to sell that same house at the current price on the market. The new buyer will then move into their house, but as a result the former owners will have been ruined because of inflation and these people are precisely those young couples of today taking commitments.
This is why I am saying that inflation and unemployment are twin brothers. Unemployment breeds inflation and inflation breeds unemployment. I have heard about that in this House since 1968. It is quite incredible to see that we are here 264 members vested with the highest authority on the land, yet we spend time talking in a lighthearted manner of these dreadful problems, not having the courage to pass measures likely to change the situation. We, from the Social Credit Party of Canada, are proposing some solutions. They may not be the best as there can always be something better but at least we have the merit of having studied the situation and of presenting concrete propositions. This is why I am asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who is not here in this House and who, I hope, will read my remarks, to have a
October 25, 1977

special study carried out by serious people on the feasibility of instituting a discount system on the domestic prices of Canadian goods.
The minister is serious, I hope. He is the one who says we are not spending enough. We are going to give consumers the chance to have more income without affecting salaries, without bearing on prices because when you raise salaries, prices go up and you are back to square one. Not so long ago an industry in my area increased salaries. A worker came and showed me his pay slip. He had $20 more on his pay but since he had changed brackets he paid more tax. So the federal government took more, the provincial government took more, the other marginal services took more, and he was finally left with $8. And since we know that prices are going to go up because of higher wages his $8 is going to be wiped out, so that is not the solution.
People are tearing at each other, union leaders point to employers as dangerous people, exploiters, and employees are being made to believe that they are mistreated and exploited, all sorts of things are put in their heads, and they are shown a dollar sign but they are not taught what an economic system is, how it works, what are the repercussions when a decision is made at given levels. They are not informed, and that is why there is social unrest, why there is no peace at home. That is why there is insecurity, why individual freedom is being restrained.
Mr. Speaker, let us give a discount on prices. Let us start with milk. We have a great milk problem at the moment in Canada. There is a legal dispute between the federal government and the provinces about the quotas and the subsidy on that part of the industrial milk coming from milk producers that goes for processing. The provinces take $1.20 for each hundredweight they collect from fluid milk producers and they must hand it over to the Canadian Dairy Commission. Since the Canadian Dairy Commission under a regulation decided to ask milk producers to give it 25 cents per hundredweight of class 1 milk and since those people say the federal government does not have the right to act like that because fluid milk comes under provincial jurisdiction, there is a conflict there. The Canadian Dairy Commission keeps the subsidies, and the Federation of Fluid Milk Producers in my province withholds the payment of the amount collected.
Mr. Speaker here is a typical example showing that if one would really stop and consider, we should utilize new methods and try this year to give a 10 cent discount on each quart of fluid milk; consumption would increase as the minister wishes, people would spend more and we would fill their needs at the family level. There is a discount if somebody buys and if nobody buys there is no discount. It is as simple as that. This is going to be the real control which will allow us to consider the problem in its true perspective. If people buy a quart of milk then they need it, and this is why they are given a 10 cent discount. The problem would be partially settled if one would stop to bickering about surpluses while other people are too poor to give the bare necessities to their families.
The Address-Mr. Cafik
Mr. Speaker, it should be possible as well to offer a discount in areas which are most vulnerable such as the shoe industry, clothing, textile, furniture which at the moment are subjected to the heaviest pressures because of more competitive imports.
So, if we gave a discount after a serious study of those products we should help businessmen be more competitive and when their warehouses would get empty following the demand from Canadians for Canadian products, automatically they would call workers back to work, thus creating employment, and we should be able to work seriously toward an answer to the employment problem. This is a practical proposal, Mr. Speaker. Here is a second one which I mentioned very briefly earlier-the establishment of an annual minimum guaranteed income to eliminate social measures that were good in the early days but that became wrong because of abuses: unemployment, social welfare, annual minimum guaranteed income based on the income, on Canadian surpluses and distributed to everyone. That annual minimum guaranteed income, Mr. Speaker, will not prevent anyone with guts to work and get an additional income. If not, if he prefers to live on that minimum it is his business. It will not prevent others from being productive and participating actively in the Canadian community.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have made very clear proposals and if we had time-unfortunately you are ready to stand up. We should also lower the age of eligibility for the old age security and make it optional at 60 for all those interested, allowing them to leave the work force and be replaced by young people.

speechtext:
1 should indicate at the outset that 1 would like to address a few remarks to the two capacities assigned to me by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when I was appointed to the cabinet. First, I was asked to act in terms of deputy House leader. 1 am very pleased and honoured to do that. I look forward with a great deal of anticipation to working with the House leaders at appropriate times to try, in the best way I know how, to make the House of Commons a relevant and responsive instrument of the wishes of the Canadian people. I am sure all House leaders, including our Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and House leader, share the intention to do whatever we can to make this place a relevant and meaningful instrument which can act expeditiously on business that is in the Canadian interest.
I want to talk more specifically about my role of minister of multiculturalism. Multiculturalism is a policy that has existed with the government of Canada for some time. 1 would like to talk about its background for just a moment. The origin of the establishment of the directorate stemmed from recommendations of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicultural-ism contained in volume IV of its report. That report dealt with contributions by other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada, and measures that should be taken to safeguard those contributions. Volume IV examined the whole question of cultural and ethnic pluralism in this country and the status of our various cultures and languages, an area of study given all too little attention in the past by scholars.
On October 8, 1971, the Prime Minister indicated, in a speech in the House of Commons, that he accepted all the recommendations contained in this commission's report. He stated that at that time:
A policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework commends itself to the government as the most suitable means of assuring the cultural freedom of Canadians. Such a policy should help to break down discriminatory attitudes and cultural jealousies. National unity if it is to mean anything in the deeply personal sense, must be founded on confidence in one's own individual identity; out of this can grow respect for that of others and a willingness to share ideas, attitudes and assumptions. A vigorous policy of multiculturalism will help create this initial confidence. It can form the base of a society which is based on fair play for all.
The government will support and encourage the various cultures and ethnic groups that give structure and vitality to our society. They will be encouraged to share their cultural expression and values with other Canadians and so contribute to a richer life for us all.
The concept of multiculturalism in the world is rather unique. To my knowledge, and based on my research, we are the first country in the world to adopt such a policy. In the last year and a half, I understand that the government of Australia, following consultations with our directorate, established a similar policy in that country. I hope the example we have given will be shared by many other countries in the future.

There is no question that multiculturalism is an extremely important concept, particularly now when there is so much talk about national unity and a feeling that the real questions facing Canadians relate to the relationship between Anglophones and Francophones.

I will leave that remark for the record; I would rather not have made it. In any event, there is no question that the public perception is that the whole equation of national unity relates to those two groups within our society.
It is very important to underscore the genuine nature of Canada. The Prime Minister has indicated in the past that we live in a bilingual nation but we do not live in a bicultural nation. It is extremely important for us to realize that distinction. Bilingualism, in the sense that we have two official languages, is, I am sure, supported by all members of this House and, if it is understood in the right context, by all Canadians. One culture is no more favoured by the government or by the people of this country than any other. All of us have brought to Canada our own unique cultural backgrounds and traditions. They need to be respected, and they are respected by this government.
Our experience in nation-building, which has been emphasized more clearly in recent days in contradistinction to the American approach, is commonly called the mosaic, as opposed to the melting pot. Many nations of the world seem to think their national interest would be better served were they to take all their cultural backgrounds and put them into some kind of melting pot from which they could be cast out into some kind of uniform shape, size and description. We subscribe to the mosaic, in the firm and consistent belief that Canada is a better place in which to live and that all of us will be better people, individually and collectively, if our people have the opportunity and the incentive to retain their cultural backgrounds, traditions and histories.
There is no doubt that our policy arises primarily from a realization of what is the full dimension of the human spirit. A great deal is said about human freedom, and it is true we need a whole broad range of freedoms; and we have them in place. But little has been said about that which gives rise to the very nature of man. Man is unique to a large extent, not only because he was created that way but because his traditions, his background, his history, his culture have all contributed to making people uniquely what they are. We believe that as a national policy we should foster this uniqueness and take advantage of it for the benefit of the whole of society.
We realize that Canadians, like all mankind, are the inheritors of the past. That makes us what we are in the present. In my view, this augurs well for the future of this country, provided we are allowed to retain that background and that history. Very special benefits flow to the whole nation and to all our people through the intermix of our culture and of our people. As a result, we build a spirit of understanding, toler-
October 25, 1977

ance and appreciation of our own individual and communal individuality. Ours is an experience in living in a real and diverse world. How well we meet this task will determine the contribution we can make by way of example to other nations and people as to how best to live together in a bilingual, multicultural and multiracial society. The world is in great need of such an example, and we as Canadians have the challenge and the privilege of setting it.
The directorate of multiculturalism and its role in our modern society seems to be viewed in three ways by the public at large. For those who support the policy, it is often viewed as a token gesture toward a third of our people of non-English, non-French backgrounds. Others who oppose the concept in principle do so on the premise that the melting pot is a more appropriate response to diversity and to national unity. Third, it is viewed with indifference by those who take our diversity for granted and who feel that present government policy is really an unnecessary instrument.
I would like to respond to these three perceptions. First of all, in terms of the view that our department might be a token effort toward multiculturalism, I would say that those who feel or think that way are confusing budgets with impact. There is no doubt at all that when one looks at the Department of Multiculturalism, realizes that we spend about $8 million a year in that area of activity, and relates that to a global budget of about $40 billion a year, one can hardly get the impression that it is other than a token gesture. However, the department is not simply a dispenser of grants to ethnocultural groups in our society; our impact is much greater than that. I shall elaborate on that aspect of the matter in a moment.
To those who have the feeling that we should not be encouraging the maintenance of our ethnocultural heritage I would like to say this: I believe they are confusing two principles, the principle of assimilation and the principle of integration. Some people think the best thing which can happen to immigrants when they come to Canada is for them to be totally assimilated into our society. To my mind, this carries with it the implication that they must shed all their background and become some new kind of human being. We do not say that at all. What we say is that they ought to be fully and totally integrated into society, realizing that their background and heritage and those things which meant so much to them as individual human beings should be freely carried on and retained here in their new land.
I think there are those who feel that the encouragement of people to retain their cultural heritage implies that we are really asking those who come from other lands to carry with them, as well, some of the antagonisms they may have developed historically in years gone by in those lands. That is not implied at all. I think it is quite evident to us that people who have come from Europe and elsewhere, where nations have shifted and changed over the years, might tend to retain antagonisms resulting from historical, cultural, linguistic and national pressures imposed upon them in their former lands. We are not asking that they do this at all. Quite the contrary. We are asking them to retain that which is good, and to shed
The Address-Mr. Cafik
and set aside those things that may have divided them back in their homelands.
I would ask those who also do not realize the import of the policy to sit back and think for a moment of some of the major cities in this country-Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and others-where you can find evidence of practically every culture of the world within their boundaries. Surely, anybody who addresses his mind to that equation would realize that those cities are richer, more vibrant than they would ever be if they did not have the input and background of the people who make up these cities.

To those who view the policy with indifference, I would say this: Operating upon a premise that I think is very easily related is the question of the English-French relationship. It is quite evident that in the past 100 years the French people, in terms of their linguistic rights and their opportunities to participate fully and totally in the whole of Canadian society, may not have been what they ought to have been. I do not think there is any question that we need a period in which to catch up in order to give them fair and equal opportunities in this country.
The same is true of our ethnocultural groups. Many of them have gone through great difficulties in years gone by in securing equal recognition, equal status with the rest of Canadians. There is a little catching up to do there as well. Immigrants are coming into this country: a great deal of work has to be done to integrate them into our society and to make sure they are given fair and equal treatment in all aspects of Canadian life. The indifference to our policy would rapidly fall aside if people realized that what we are trying to do with these groups which have come into the country, whose ancestors came here hundreds of years ago, is to make sure they are provided with a fair and equal opportunity along with the rest of us.
There is another point I want to make in this respect. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, the percentage make up of our society. First of all, about 43 per cent of our population has an Anglo-Celtic background. The figures I am giving are not easily defined or even accurate statistics, but they are reasonably close. The French-speaking group constitutes about 25 per cent or a little more. Our native peoples comprise about 2 per cent of our population. Other ethnocultural groups account for the remaining 30 per cent. It is my job as Minister of State for Multiculturalism to see that all groups in our society are given fair and equal opportunity in this land. I think it is important that we carry out that mandate in all the broad ranges of human activity.
The legitimate, important and indeed essential role of the directorate of multiculturalism I think bears some explanation. First of all, in relation to grants, I mentioned earlier that we have a number of grants programs. We distribute about $4.5 million to $5 million a year to ethnocultural groups in Canada.

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. Cafik
I should like to make one thing quite clear. I am not of the view that it is necessary for the government of Canada to preserve culture in the sense that we require money to do so. I am inclined to think that cultures that are real, alive and viable would sustain themselves if we spent $1 billion a year trying to uproot them. The fact is that they are cultures because people want them. They are sustained because people want them.
Our granting funds to these groups is not really directed to that objective. Our funds are granted in a different way altogether, to provide equal opportunity; but, in addition, to make sure that all Canadians share in the benefits of those cultures. This enables cultural groups to work and to interface together, to share their backgrounds and traditions with all of the community in which they live. In that way that which is theirs will become that which is ours, and all of us will benefit as a result.
I am not suggesting that the real thrust of our department is in the form of grants, as important as they may be. They will be sustained in areas where they are required. The real impact of the Department of Multiculturalism is more global; it has an impact upon government policy as a whole. It seems to me that when the government gives consideration to policies, of whatever description, in so far as they impinge upon the interests of those people who are within my mandate it is my responsibility, in the halls of cabinet and in the decision-making process, to see that their legitimate views and concerns are taken into account.
Dealing with specific issues is also important. For example, international human rights arising from the Helsinki Accord and now being dealt with at the Belgrade conference are a matter of genuine and serious concern to many people who come from behind iron curtain countries or from the Soviet Union itself. 1, as the representative of those people, must ensure that their voice is heard by those who make decisions regarding our posture at the Belgrade conference. The same thing occurs with regard to immigration policy, citizenship and the broad range of government policy. So the impact of the directorate of multiculturalism is broader than grants of money; it is as broad as the government itself.
We also have to deal directly with domestic perceptions which lead to mutual recognition and respect among all Canadians. There is no question that difficulties arise from time to time as a result of intolerance, lack of understanding and lack of appreciation of the backgrounds and traditions of others. It is extremely important that our directorate deals positively with those difficulties to ensure that we have an orderly integration of all people in society, leaving them the option, indeed the right, to be themselves in every way they can.
In addition, it is the responsibility of the directorate to try to give Canadians a more accurate reflection of ourselves and our backgrounds. First of all, in looking at our educational institutions-which are out of our jurisdiction-the media, the composition of our libraries and museums, politics, the arts and the whole broad range of human activities, it is very important

that we begin to portray ourselves for what we are, a multicultural, multiracial society with each group having made a valuable and important historical contribution.
It is not enough to look upon the history of Canada as beginning and ending with the Plains of Abraham. It is important that we know the contribution of the Ukrainians in western Canada, the Germans in western Canada, the Japanese on the west coast, the Polish, the Irish-everyone. It is in that context that we will begin to understand what Canada is really all about. I think our institutions of all types have an obligation to address themselves to this question and not spend so much of their time dealing only with English-French relations in Canada, which I think gives a distorted picture of our reality.
The key to a successful policy is to ensure that all of us, individually and collectively, are better off if we recognize and take advantage of our own background and diversity, allowing it to flower so that the public interest may be best achieved. Each of us as Canadians, regardless of our origin, will become richer and more vital because of the interface between our culture and the culture of other groups. Through it we will draw the maximum benefit and create a wholesome and vibrant society. It is not our intention to build a nation of isolated solitudes. The key element in our program is to bring together individual cultures working in combination with others and impacting upon the whole community.
Those of ethnocultural backgrounds have a great interest in the national unity question. Perhaps they realize as much as, or more than, anyone what is at stake in this issue. Our ethnocultural groups can readily identify and understand the aspirations of the people of Quebec to preserve their language and their culture. We accept the concept of bilingualism and we support the legitimate concerns of French-speaking Canadians in regard to the preservation of their culture and language. Their aspirations are not unlike our own, and for that reason we find it so easy to relate to that concept.
We can also understand the concern of many in the province of Quebec that their cultural background could possibly be totally absorbed by the English society either within their province or outside. We understand the need and the desire to take steps to retain that which they have, that which they are so proud of, and with good reason. So we support this policy. We support the policy of bilingualism and the right of the people of Quebec and of other provinces to retain that which is theirs in the context of free choice and under the banner of two official languages. We believe it is important that all Canadians have the right to communicate with their government in either of the official languages, wherever they reside in this country.
1 do not wish to deal with bill 101 at any length, except to say that it is my view the questions at stake are not really legal ones. I believe this is the view of many Canadians. The question of national unity will not be resolved in the Supreme Court of Canada; it will be resolved in the hearts and minds of
October 25, 1977

Canadians. Any society which is united, is united because it wants to be united and because its people realize that they are better off culturally, economically, linguistically and in every other way if they are united.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Our people realize we are better off being Canadians with a whole Canada, as opposed to separating this country into individual parts. It would not be in the interests of any Canadian to allow that to happen. We must all show that we recognize our interdependence. But even more, we must show that we recognize our mutual good will toward each other. Our national unity problem shall disappear when Francophones, Anglophones, our native peoples and our ethnocultural groups of any origin fully realize that we are all better off economically, socially, culturally and linguistically if we are living in one land in a spirit of understanding, tolerance and good will. When this realization takes root in Canadians in every corner of our land from the Pacific to the Atlantic and from the American border to the North Pole, we shall indeed be a free, happy and united nation showing leadership in a divided and often antagonistic world.
It is only by the realization of that which makes us what we are, uniquely Canadian, that those aspirations can be achieved.
I assure all members of this House that the ethnocultural communities of this country are as married to that concept as any other group-perhaps more than some. We will play our part in holding this country together and building it to be the land we want to decree to our children.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. For certain obvious reasons, this was a very special throne speech, since it was only the second time in our nation's history that the speech was read by a reigning monarch. It was special, as well, because the occasion surrounding this particular event was the Silver Jubilee of our Queen, and her visit to Canada encompassed our tribute to Her Majesty's 25-year reign.
Therefore, it is regrettable that the content of the Speech from the Throne did not match the uniqueness of the occasion surrounding it. If it were not so tragic, it would be almost humorous that such regal pomp and ceremony should surround such a limited, pedestrian document. The speech was not what the times demanded.
1 think back to that other occasion some 20 years ago when Her Majesty participated in a similar ceremony, and I speak to the Canada of that era. Those of us who remember that occasion can remember, also, the optimism, the buoyancy and the stability which marked those years. Then our world, globally and domestically, was relatively stable. At that time we believed-and our belief was confirmed by reality-that if we worked hard, we would achieve. We told our children that those who stayed in school, studied hard and graduated would have a job waiting for them when they finished their education. Those were the rules of the game, and no one doubted them.
The realities of today dramatically call into question those hopes and beliefs. The buoyancy and the optimism of the fifties have dissipated into instability, fear and uncertainty in the seventies. It is the uncertainty, the lack of confidence

permeating this country, that is the most destructive of the moods of the seventies. Instability can be coped with if there is some certainty that it will be eased, whether sooner or later. A nation's fears can be calmed if there is certainty that there are clear choices to be made and competent people to make them. But there is no solace in uncertainty. Uncertainty can bring on needless fear and increased instability. Uncertainty can smother hope.
Whatever else are its accomplishments, this government is a past master at creating uncertainty. In no other field has it been so productive, and with what disastrous effects for the nation! The current uncertainty, in the face of economic controls and controversial constitutional questions, is only the tip of the iceberg which has been in the process of formation for these past ten years. The proposals put forth last week in the Speech from the Throne do nothing to counteract that mood of uncertainty or to restore the confidence of Canadians. Quite the contrary, it does everything to add to our collective uncertainty since, by spelling out the many problems that face us, it confirms our worst fears; and then, by offering what are patently facile and superficial remedies, it invites our despair. It is true that the government recognizes the current economic crisis: it is right there in the speech from the throne. It reads:
High rates of unemployment and inflation are clear signals of the inadequacy of economic strategies . .. signals of the urgent need for important structural adjustments in the economy .. .
Sir, since the throne speech, we have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and we have heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) discuss the economy at great length. But what we have yet to hear in concrete terms are the so-called important structural adjustments that the government intends to make to the economy. The government's announcement of a proposed expenditure of $150 million in job creation is one of the few concrete proposals put forth. But what does that really represent? A mere 60,000 jobs for the one million Canadians who are without work. Such a proposal can hardly be considered an important structural adjustment. Major structural adjustments are necessary if the government is to confront, not just the hard economic realities that we in the opposition keep bringing to their attention every day but the social cost of these realities.
1 would like the Prime Minister and his colleagues to look back for a moment on their own lives and remember the dreams and ambitions of their youth, to realize how much the existence of possibilities contributed to their hopes, their choices and to the options that were open to them. For the unemployed youth of today, possibilities, choices or options are practically non-existent. Not only do they not have jobs, costly as that is to the economy, but, furthermore, 400,000 young Canadians are unable to make the crucial decisions that are necessary to shape their futures. They cannot plan their lives, nor can they dream, wildly or otherwise, about their future.
What does it do to their personal development, to their self-worth, to be so unable to control their lives? What will the possible cost to our society of the collective cynicism of a
October 25, 1977

generation which has played the game by the rules only to find that the rules have changed at the end? I would ask the Prime Minister to consider that we are facing the possibility of producing a generation of adults who have been totally alienated from the mainstream of Canadian life. Such alienation can only bring anger and frustration in its wake, but more than anger and frustration, social upheaval of a kind that we have not witnessed in Canada previously. We in this country are not immune to the social unrest that is emerging elsewhere in the world, an unrest that our current unemployment situation does nothing to stave off and everything to invite.
Mr. Speaker, there are no major structural changes recommended in the Speech from the Throne to indicate that the government either recognizes or plans to take steps to alleviate these serious social pressures. It is very easy to conclude, in the wake of what we have heard, that the best structural change that could be made, the one most beneficial to this country, would be to get rid of the present government.

If the economic measures in the Speech from the Throne offer little to quell the climate of uncertainty that exists in this country, the constitutional proposals offer even less. Indeed, in his collective musings on our constitutional problems, the Prime Minister escalates the uncertainty that abounds with his apparently off-the-cuff suggestion without benefit of cabinet decision.
It would appear that the government may hold a referendum on national unity, and I stress the word "may" because, true to form, the Prime Minister declines to give any details of his proposed referendum. He equivocates. The referendum may or may not be held; it may or may not be held nationally; it may or may not be held only in Quebec. If held in Quebec, it may or may not be binding on that province or on the rest of the country. The Prime Minister mounts a horse called "referendum" and then he rides off in all directions. A referendum if necessary, but not necessarily a referendum. The Prime Minister, by his lack of precision in this matter, seems determined to add another dimension to the uncertainty of our present constitutional crisis.
Our fragile federal system is already sorely beset by fears and anxieties. Those of us who are profoundly concerned about the future of our country-that includes members of all sides of the House-are concerned lest the Prime Minister's conflicting comments of the past few days will add to those fears and uncertainties. Surely, it is the height of irresponsibility for a prime minister to introduce such a far-reaching proposal without any indication of how he intends to implement it. Surely, it is totally irresponsible and an abuse of the office of prime minister to propose in the House a serious measure that could involve very basic changes in our parliamentary system, and then shroud the proposal in circumlocution and speculation. One has to ask oneself if this referendum-cum-plebiscite, or plebiscite-cum-referendum, is no more than a diversionary tactic designed to take the attention of the people of this
The Address-Miss MacDonald
country away from the government's inept handling of economic problems.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not only does the Prime Minister's penchant for musing aloud on such a serious matter serve to distort the function of the House; in addition, his subsequent allusion to unilateral action on the constitution which could result from such a referendum seriously undermines and ignores the role of the premiers of the provinces in constitutional reform. At this time of crisis, both economic and constitutional, it is of the utmost importance that the partners in confederation work together and not at cross-purposes. Does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) seriously believe the announcement one day of his intention to visit each premier to discuss constitutional matters, and his allusion the following day to the possibility of unilateral action on the constitution, is the kind of initiative that is conducive to co-operation?
The Prime Minister should recognize that the process of conducting federal-provincial relations requires as much sensitivity and as much consideration as do the substantive measures involved. A viable confederation capable of adapting to the natural forces of social and economic change rests on a process of continuous federal-provincial consultation and accommodation. To be effective, this process of accommodation requires mutual respect and trust between the federal government and the provincial governments. When that trust and respect does not exist, tensions arise which emphasize our differences rather than our common interests.
The conduct of the federal Liberal government in dealings with the provinces over the last ten years has imposed a serious additional strain on national unity. One has only to look at the federal government's record of federal-provincial relations to see this strain. The reluctance of the provinces to enter into negotiations in resource development and the failure of the federal government to produce agreement in the area of social security revenue, after four years of negotiation, are but two examples of the deterioration in intergovernmental affairs that have had direct and, indeed, negative results on the level of services and the prosperity that Canadians should enjoy in this country. These results, in turn, have a direct bearing on weakening the national fabric of our country.
In short, the process of federal-provincial relations over the last ten years-that process itself-has adversely affected the ability of governments to act as a unit. The approach of the present federal government has been to treat the provinces and provincial aspirations as a problem that can only be solved by the central government.
In contrast to this approach, the leader of my party and the then four Progressive Conservative premiers met recently at Kingston and produced, with unanimity, a program for economic recovery and federal-provincial reconciliation. The reason that agreement was produced among leaders with extremely diverse constituencies stems from a fundamentally

October 25, 1977
The Address-Miss MacDonald different approach from that of the government to federal-provincial relations and federalism. The first reason that agreement was reached was that agreement, rather than confrontation, was sought. The second and more important reason was, and is, because the Progressive Conservative party recognizes that provincial governments must be assured that their interests will be recognized and integrated into the development of national policy.
In speaking of the Kingston conference, the Prime Minister attempted in his speech last week to make light of the achievements of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Conservative Premiers regarding entrenchment of equalization payments in the constitution-a proposal, I may say, far more specific and fundamental than that proposed by the Prime Minister at Victoria, or any since. In fact, the latest effort along these lines that the Prime Minister can point to on the part of his government occurred last year during an early stage in the federal-provincial fiscal negotiations, when a major change in the revenue equalization formula was proposed which, if it had been carried out, would have significantly weakened the basic purpose of equalization and created new regional inequities.
Contrast this with the initiative taken at Kingston for the full and formal protection of revenue equalization in the constitution. This initiative was taken by, among others, the Premiers of the two wealthiest provinces as being right and just in the building and maintaining of a sense of national community.
That was one initiative taken at Kingston. There were others: a commitment to annual consultation among first ministers on economic and fiscal policies and goals, so that fiscal decisions taken by one level of government do not distort and frustrate the policies and objectives of the other; a commitment to patriation of the constitution and to the involvement of provincial governments in appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada, a proportion of those to the Senate and such agencies as the Canadian Transport Commission and the National Energy Board, so as to assure the federal nature of these institutions. There was much more.
The Prime Minister not only belittled these initiatives but, as well, sought to distort the position of those at that conference regarding minority language rights in the constitution, a position based on the agreement arrived at by nine of the provincial Premiers at St. Andrew's earlier this year, and endorsed in Kingston.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All proposed at Victoria.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That kind of tactic, of course, should not surprise us. For ten years the Prime Minister has been unrelenting in his deliberate efforts to distort the position of this party regarding the official languages policy, to create suspicion and breed distrust and, to his shame, he does it in the name of national unity. What probably goads the Prime Minister into this reaction is the fact that after his own many attempts ended in failure, the Leader of the Opposition was able to sit down with four provincial Premiers and arrive at

specific, concrete proposals in relation to the problems facing Canadians. The Prime Minister offers us vague generalizations based on his own proposals. The Leader of the Opposition offers concrete commitments based on discussion and agreement with his provincial counterparts: that is the difference.
In a similar vein, I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister's petty reaction towards the Kingston conference is further reflected in his negative attitude toward calling a federal-provincial first ministers' conference both on the problems of national unity and on the problems of the economy.
Some years ago, at the Victoria conference, the Prime Minister proposed that the first ministers of this country meet annually to discuss matters of federal-provincial concern. Since then, the Prime Minister and the Premiers have met every year, and in some years have met two or even three times on matters of urgency. The proposal of 1971 had become a reality-until this year. This year, the year in which the problems that we face have reached crisis proportions, is the only year since 1971 that a federal-provincial conference of first ministers has not been held. The Premier of Ontario has called for one, the Premier of New Brunswick has called for one; and all the Prime Minister will tell us is that he intends to visit the Premiers individually in the near future and that he may or may not call a federal-provincial conference at some future time. The institution of the first ministers' meetings is an integral part of our system, particularly in dealing with constitutional matters. It deserves to be honoured by the Prime Minister. But, instead, he chooses the route of bilateral negotiations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Instead, he chooses to go and see each of them personally, directly and face-to-face.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We see the pattern emerging, Mr. Speaker: the Prime Minister believes that he, and he alone, has the right to deal with the issue of national unity. Yet in the 11 months since the election of the Parti Quebecois government, his initiatives have been negligible, his actions few.
The Premiers meet, and nine of them reach accord. The Leader of the Opposition and his provincial counterparts meet and work out specific proposals. Meanwhile, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) meditates. He carps about and ridicules the actions of others. But for a year he has existed in a state of semi-paralysis. He neglects the cabinet in his plan for a referendum. He belittles the efforts of opposition leaders. He ignores the calls of the provincial Premiers for a federal-provincial conference; and of most importance to this chamber, he spurns the establishment of an all-party parliamentary committee on national unity. None of the established institutions in this country for dealing with constitutional crisis merit his consideration.
1 remind the Prime Minister that certain issues, because of their gravity and universality, transcend the normal bounds of
October 25, 1977

partisan politics. The question of national unity and constitutional reform is such an issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I have never heard a more partisan speech.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Were the Prime Minister to show half the respect he should to established procedures and institutions, he would begin by immediately setting up a parliamentary committee to deal with national unity. This party has been demanding such a committee for a long time; but, true to form, the Prime Minister has not heeded such a proposal.
If the Prime Minister cannot accept this recommendation from the opposition, perhaps he might listen to the views of a former Liberal cabinet minister-and there are lots of those. Perhaps he would listen to the views of a man who was asked by the Prime Minister himself to serve on his personal task force on national unity, but who declined. I refer to Claude Castonguay. There was a great deal of speculation at the time as to why Mr. Castonguay rejected the Prime Minister's invitation to join his task force. Well, now we know the reason. Mr. Castonguay felt-indeed, he knew-that there was a more appropriate vehicle. In speaking to the University of Toronto's recent Options Conference, he said that the parliament of Canada and each provincial legislature should form a committee composed of members from every political party.
Mr. Castonguay suggested that these broadly based committees could hear briefs from interested groups and members of the public and conduct their own studies. Then they could formulate proposals for reform. Mr. Castonguay also suggested that implementation of this approach would also depolarize the Trudeau-Levesque debate and put an end to its sterility. It would provide a forum for the majority of Quebeckers who want change but who do not seek independence. That is the advice from a former leading Liberal.
We, the Progressive Conservative members of the opposition, have been calling for such a committee at the federal level, to no avail. We called for it in the House this past summer and were told at that time by the Prime Minister that we were too far into the session to establish such a committee. Would the Prime Minister care to tell us now that we are too far into this session to establish a committee? Will he offer us another excuse, or will he admit that the representation of all parties in the crucial debate on national unity is both necessary and desirable; and will he give assurances that he will act to set up such a committee?
How long does this troubled country have to wait for its Prime Minister to avail himself of the avenues open to him on this issue? How long is the cancer of uncertainty to be nurtured by his neglect? When will this country again be able to look with confidence to its government and with hope to its future? The Speech from the Throne, and the Prime Minister's discourse which followed it, have shown clearly that there is no hope that this will happen in this session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if someone were to ask me if Canada has any enemies, I would have to say it has. I would say that I even know the names of those
The Address-Mrs. Appolloni
enemies. They are discord, defeatism, despondency and despair-and anyone who arms those enemies does no service to Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to quote three short paragraphs from the Speech from the Throne;
It can be an era of increasing confrontation, tension and division, or an era of enhanced freedom, cooperation and unity of purpose. Fundamentally, the choice must be made by every citizen every day.
It is apparent to thoughtful Canadians everywhere that this is a time of great decisions for Canada, a time for rediscovering the strength and potential of a marvellously free and caring society.
That rediscovery will require that Canadians rededicate themselves to each other's well-being-
Those are beautiful words in any language, and they sounded much more meaningful because they came from the lips of Her Majesty the Queen, who has shown to us her own personal warmth and sincerity. But words, no matter how beautiful, can be cruel shams unless they are transmitted into action.
I read an article in the Globe and Mail recently. It was a survey of several members of parliament, including myself. It said that there seems to be a feeling among some constituents that the problem we are having with Quebec does not affect every Canadian, that it is something just between our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the leader of the Parti Quebecois, or that it is something just between Ottawa and Quebec, as if it were another tragic "tale of two cities". Those constituents felt it did not concern them; that is the way the newspaper reported it. But I am beginning to wonder if the attitude of those constituents did not reflect some feeling of personal helplessness rather than indifference. What can the individual Canadian do? 1 would like to offer only a few suggestions, because time does not allow me to offer very many. But I hope they are constructive ones.
If the problem in Quebec or with our French-speaking brothers were only a question between two leaders, a kind of one-upmanship, or a question of who is better than the other, I would probably be like everybody else and say that we should sit back and let them fight, knowing very well that one of them would get a bloodied nose. However, it is more than that. If it was a question of two provinces, I would probably say, "Why worry? Let Bill Davis and Rene Levesque fight it out. Why should l get involved?"
However, the whole point is that we are not talking about some little fight or about one-upmanship; What is at stake in this whole tragedy is our destiny and, more importantly, the destiny of our children. Are they going to grow up as citizens of one great, united country, or are they going to grow up in a fragmented society? That is what is at stake. We must assure ourselves, as individuals, that what is at stake is too important to be left to two men, two cities or even to two provinces and each and every one of us has to get involved. How? I thought about that. Again, something happened quite recently. It was the granting of the Nobel Peace prize. While it was for 1976, it was only given a couple of days ago. I read the citation, which is as follows:

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mrs. Appolloni
Mairad Corrigan and Betty Williams acted out of a deep conviction that individual people can do meaningful efforts for peace through conciliatory work.
I put the emphasis on "individual people". When I read that, I decided to find out as much as I could about these two women. Who were they? Did they have some tremendous academic distinction? Are they supported by big government, big management or big labour? Who is behind them? When I did my research, I found out that nobody was supporting them. When asked how they got started, one is reported to have said, "Someone had to get up and do something."
I am not intending to draw analogies between the situation in Northern Ireland and the situation we have here with our French-speaking brothers. I am the first to pray that our differences in this country will never escalate to the type of holocaust that has occurred in Northern Ireland. That is not the similarity. The similarity is what that woman who received the Nobel prize for peace demonstrated. Somebody has to stand up and do something. What a marvellous spirit! That is the kind of spirit that appeals to me. It is the kind of spirit I understand. It is the kind of spirit that is mentioned in the Speech from the Throne and what I want it to be-the Canadian spirit.
What can each and every one of us individually do for our country, not only with regard to political problems but economic problems? Let us start with the political problems. What can we do? If I may, I will address myself primarily to the women of Canada. They are 50 per cent of the population; therefore, we have a very vested interest in this question. What would I, as a woman of Canada, do in this particular situation? I would start by speaking to my French-speaking sisters. I would tell them we have a tremendous amount in common. Like me, most of them are mothers. They have the same aspirations for their children as I have for mine. Their children try just as hard as mine. There is no difference there.
I would then have to be very honest and say to them that mistakes were made in the past. I would tell them that I am really sorry that some time ago, even in the near distant past, their kids had to learn my language before they could communicate with government, theirs and mine. I would say that I am sorry there were other inequities as well. I would then say that things have improved. They really have. I will tell you why I say that. My favourite five-year old sibling is now going through French kindergarten in Toronto. I emphasize, in Toronto, Mr. Speaker. His parents could not do that because they did not have that opportunity. His little brother will go. The time will come when he will go to his French-speaking cousins and feel at home. That is the way it should be.
I would have to say to my sisters in Quebec that they know as well as I do that two wrongs do not make a right. I would have to say that what their leaders are now suggesting is a repetition of past errors. They are saying that if my children go to Quebec, they cannot continue in their language. That is exactly what happened in the past with their kids. They do not want that to happen. My French sisters would probably tell me that it is not just language; there is an awful lot more involved.

I would be the first to agree with that. We do not know about their culture, but what are we going to do? Here, again, I would tell them that things are improving.
A few years ago I telephoned a large radio station in Toronto. I spoke to the disc jockey. I told him 1 liked the music he played, but it saddened me a bit because I never heard music from Quebec. He said they could not play it because no one understood the words. What a lot of boloney! Things have improved. When in Toronto last week, I put on the car radio. The first thing 1 heard was pop music from Quebec. It was great. We cannot accept the phony argument that no one understands the words. Italian and German opera has been heard and loved throughout the world. People do not know the words, but they do not care; they get the feeling of the music, and they love it. A disc jockey might say, with regard to pop music, that it is the lyrics that count. That, too, is a phony, specious argument. You cannot understand most of the words in today's pop music. It is not the king's English, but gibberish. Who cares; the kids like it.
What can we do? We can telephone our radio stations, not just in Ontario and Manitoba but throughout English-speaking Canada, and tell them we believe we are getting a raw deal, that we have heard that the best pop music comes out of Quebec and we want to hear it. We would not do this in order to patronize. Nobody wants to be patronized. It must be because we have heard that it is the best in this part of the world. Somebody has to get up and do something. My Frenchspeaking sisters would say that it is not just language or even just culture, but a lot of other things. My kids are learning French. I am going to make sure they get the benefit of hearing that music, not just to be good to those in Quebec, because that would be silly, but because that music is great. By listening to their records, not only do we get a bit of Quebec-which is a great feeling-but it helps their recording industry. That is the kind of co-operation I would like to stress.
Let us go on to what individuals can do to help, not only the political problems we face at this time but the economic problems. Maybe it is very difficult to divorce one from the other. Here, again, there is much the individual can do. We must realize that the realities of the situation have changed. Now, more than ever, our economy is in a period of transition. Things will never be the same again. We can no longer feel ourselves fortunate because we have so many natural resources at our disposal. We still have them; however, we must realize they are not infinite, but finite. We have to husband them with very great care. No longer can we use oil and electricity as though it will be here forever.
We must individually examine what we do in our own houses. Do we really need all those lights turned on? I am looking around the chamber. I assume that we need all these lights. Apart from the tremendous consumption of energy, they are awfully hard on the eyes. There are many things we can do in our own houses. We have to be very sensible about our energy supplies. We know without doubt that they are finite. Everyone must do his share. I have not been used to this tremendous affluence of energy supplies. It is difficult to
October 25, 1977

suddenly change all one's habits. What we need is not just somebody saying, "Okay; you have to conserve energy; you have to do this and that". This is not enough. You have to motivate people.
I should like to use a word which is not often used any more, and 1 regret it. I should like to say-and this refers to motivation, "Save energy because it is patriotic to do so". There is nothing wrong with being patriotic. I wish we would show a little more of it. Not patriotism of the old type. We are not going back to Rudyard Kipling and fifes and drums. We are not going to ask people to die for their country; we are going to ask them to live for their country. That is the motivation. Let us conserve what we have very carefully. Then, once we have looked at our own houses, let us go out in our community and find out what our municipalities are doing. For instance, how are they treating the disposal systems? Are they doing enough? Then we could turn to the province and finally to the federal government.
We are all vitally interested in this idea of energy conservation. Can we afford to have so much waste? Could we not think more about the advantages of recycling? Jobs are being lost daily. That is a terrible tragedy. But the day will come- hopefully, very soon-when we shall hear that though the old jobs are being lost, new jobs are being created, but not by the government, Mr. Speaker; not by the government.
