speechtext: Elear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You hear people say, "I should like to do this", or, "1 should like to do that". I ask them why they do not go out and do it, and they reply, "Too much intervention from all levels of government". I say to them, "If you really believe that any level of government is putting a stranglehold on your ability to do things as an individual, I would tell that government to butt out. But once you tell it to butt out by one door, don't ask it to come back through another".
We are still talking about the individual. What can an individual do to help the economy?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why not the government?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. member why. It is because I firmly believe it is the sum of individual effort which leads in the long run to the success of the collectivity. It is the individual who matters. That is what our society is all about. It is not what society can do for the individual, but vice versa. Here, again, I speak from the point of view of members of my own sex because they hold the purse strings. Go into any supermarket in this town or in my own city of Toronto and you will find, for example, that the lamb on sale comes from New Zealand or Australia. 1 am not talking about the balance of trade; we all know there must be a certain balance of trade between ourselves and our trading partners. What is it like, this lamb from New Zealand or Australia? It is fatty and indigestible. You wonder why you buy it. When you ask about Canadian lamb, you are told there is not enough Canadian
The Address-Mrs. Appolloni
production. Why not, Mr. Speaker? Then you go into a Greek restaurant in Toronto and you find the lamb is exquisite. What is the difference? Do you know what it is? That lamb is prime lamb from the fields of Ontario.
What about McDonald's? One should thank them for coming into our country, bringing in their capital and providing a certain number of jobs. But ask them where the beef which goes into their patties comes from. Is it grown in Alberta? If they say it is Australian, ask them why they are not using Canadian beef.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Don't forget Canadian wine.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When was the last time you tasted Canadian wine with your hamburger or lamb, or whatever you eat? By jove-just like the pop music from Quebec, I can guarantee it is darned good.
What else can we do? Look at the souvenirs sold at Niagara Falls. Maybe you want to buy something to remind you of your trip. Do you know what it is likely to be? A very nasty, gaudy bauble, and if you look closely at it you will find it was made in Hong Kong or some other place abroad.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is the same everywhere.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No; there are other places. I will give out a free advertisement. Go into the Davis Agency here, or the Four Corners store, most places around Ottawa, and you will find tasteful Canadian-made things at reasonable prices. These are just a few ideas about what individual consumers can do. 1 suggest that every week when families are checking the shopping list, they should make another column in which to list the country of origin of the items they buy. This is important. We have to help our economy. I know we shall face criticism. Someone will accuse us of narrow self-interest. Like heck! Any neighbour who is a good neighbour will realize that the family comes first. This is the Canadian family, and it has to come first. I am not saying anybody should buy shoddy goods. Such goods deserve to be passed over. But in my experience Canadian goods are not shoddy. Maybe we have not given them the support they deserve. Let us buy all the Canadian-made goods we can.
There is still more to be done. Take the fish we put into our children's sandwiches when they go to school. Where was it canned? If it was canned in British Columbia, and other things are equal, let us by all means buy the product which was canned in British Columbia. If we find that many of the things we want to buy are not made in this country, we shall have to ask ourselves some very serious questions. I am not talking now about goods which cannot be produced here for climatic or similar reasons.
I have been trying all day to find out whether a rumour I have heard is true. The rumour is that only two pulp and paper mills in this country make cartons for milk. 1 can hardly believe it, since almost every day we see in the newspapers big advertisements inserted by the pulp and paper industry of Canada telling us that they are in trouble. So I have been

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mrs. Appolloni
trying to find out what percentage of the milk cartons used in Canada are actually made in this country. I was not able to get a precise answer. What I did get was the information that only 5 per cent of all corrugated paper used in Canada is manufactured in Canada. In other words, with all the forests at our disposal, we only corner 5 per cent of that market. Why do we not have more? Processing paper means more jobs. It is not that we are not capable of processing paper; we can do that and many more things. Is it because our people have a little less courage than others? Let us ask ourselves all these questions, Mr. Speaker.
Still on the economy, I would tell the average Mr. or Mrs. Canadian to be very careful how their representatives negotiate for them in the upcoming GATT agreements. I would tell them that we all know that an industry which is not competitive or efficient does not deserve to be supported. On the other hand, we must be extremely careful to make a distinction, if I may use a very familiar simile, between the child, the infant just learning to crawl, and the lazy teenager. If our infant, our industry, is just learning to crawl, you cannot automatically enter it in a four-mile marathon. We cannot afford to do that. We cannot afford to be the Boy Scouts of the world, even though Canada is great and open. I wonder if the others are as open as we are. What about the absence of tariff barriers on goods from other countries? In the meantime, our people are without jobs. So I say, watch the GATT agreements.
Now the future. At the moment we have a tremendous number of Cassandras-economic Cassandras and media Cas-sandras. It seems to be the great thing these days to say, "Oh, boy, you're going down the drain!" This is not doing us any service at all. What we need now are torchbearers of hope and confidence, and by jove we can have them. As for the future, it is going to be different, vastly different, from the past. It is not going to be an extension of the past, mainly because of our natural resources but also for other reasons. I think we will have to diversify. We will have to use all the imagination, enthusiasm and initiative of which we are capable. We can make the future a better, more humane place, we can have a better environment, if we have proper planning and design and the collective will.
We very definitely have problems, but we cannot allow them to come so near to us that they obstruct or even obliterate our vision. That would be foolhardy and tragic. I should like to refer to a recent report by the Science Council of Canada entitled "Canada as a Conserver Society". It tells us that the future can very well be much, much better than the present, but to what degree will depend upon whether we face the change with inertia, or grapple the challenges with all the enthusiasm, imagination and initiative of which we are capable.
Our long-term policy will be to achieve reliance on sources of renewable energy, aided by improvements in conservation and efficiency. New technologies such as solar heating, electricity from wind and liquid fuels from biomass will probably

be developed economically and on a scale sufficient to meet new demands. The challenge is there, and we have the technology at our disposal. My time is up, Mr. Speaker, but my views are not.

subtopic: SPEECH FROM THE THRONE
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should first like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. As individuals they made a valuable contribution, and I do not blame them for the misdeeds of the government opposite which I am going to speak about in a few minutes.
I want to speak this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, as a torch-bearer of hope-the hope this government is going out of office in 1978 and that this country will get on its feet again. I do not believe that what we heard at the opening of this session was a Speech from the Throne. It was a whisper from the throne. It was a whimper from the throne. It was a plea for sympathy from the throne. It was a whine for forgiveness from the throne. It was a subtle and subliminal attempt to "con" all Canadians into believing that they, individually, are to blame for the state of Canada today, not this great wonderful government which sits opposite and which has occupied the benches of power and authority in this House for the last nine years.
October 25, 1977

That is what the Speech from the Throne was designed to do, Mr. Speaker, but it has fooled no one. Despite the fact that it was delivered by Her Majesty the Queen, its content is insipid, to say the least, and its intent is insidious, to say the best. What have we had after nine years? Canada brought to its knees. I do not want to bore the House with figures, but briefly they show that in 1968 the national unemployment rate was 4.5 per cent. In 1967, the year before, it was 3.8 per cent. Today, it is 8.3 per cent-far worse in eastern Canada. In 1968, the inflation rate was 50 per cent less than the present rate of 8.3 per cent. It has doubled since 1968. This year, real economic growth is 2 per cent. That is the best that Pierre can do for economic growth in Canada.
The government's budgetary deficit is $9.2 billion. When I was minister of finance in Newfoundland I thought, "My God how can I ever survive?" But our deficits were not even a twinkle in the eye of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) when compared to this government's deficit of $9.2 billion. Revenue was only $33 billion 50 million. In addition, to such a deficit, hundreds of thousands of Canadians are unemployed; and everyone is suffering from inflation. We have a trade deficit in the billions. We have a Canadian dollar worth 89 decimal point something cents in terms of the U.S. dollar.
Do hon. members remember the "Diefendollar" and how the right hon. member was jeered at, this great man who sits with us on the front benches today? Now we have the floating dollar. It does not matter that it is worth 89 cents; the great answer of those on the benches opposite is that it is a floating dollar. They are very proud of what they call this floating dollar, is like a floating rib or a floating kidney. It is something which was invented by the Liberals and is supposed to be magnificent.
Well, Mr. Speaker, as our leader said the other day, the floating dollar has sprung a leak; we have a pretty leaky floating dollar. It is a Liberal leak. It is an 89-cent dollar, and some experts think it is going down to 85 cents or possibly 80 cents before it comes up again. That is where this government has brought us.
Then we have this pitiful attempt at a budget which was brought in under the Speech from the Throne. I refer to it as a gay budget, because it was sneaked in the back door! It was not brought out like a properly married woman. It was hidden and sneaked into the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is a queer budget. That is where the government has brought us.
National unity is the great Liberal security blanket. They think we are all going to go to sleep worried about national unity, and vote them back into office in 1978. Not a hope! The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) cannot lead us to national unity. He has had nine years since being elected into office in 1968. He was elected on the promise of national unity and bilingualism. Where has he led us? Now he wants a confrontation so that he can get on our backs for another five years. Not likely!
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
Hon. cabinet ministers do not need to suck their thumbs. They have the national unity security blanket to get under every night. That will not work for them. That is the direction in which this country has been led.
A prominent Canadian, the ex-premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Joseph Smallwood, has a solution to the national unity question. 1 should like to quote from an article which appeared in a New Brunswick newspaper several months ago. It reads as follows:
... the only way to keep Quebec in Canada is for English-speaking Canadians to "smother Quebecers with love."
1 would not mind doing that in our caucus because there are only two to go. But it would wipe out the Liberal government opposite if we smothered them with love. That is the solution which was proposed by Mr. Smallwood, that we have to smother the Quebecers with love. Our two had better watch out if that advice is taken.
That is the kind of crap and nonsense which is coming from Liberals across this nation with regard to national unity. We are supposed to keep our mouths shut, listen to them, and believe that only they have the answers to these problems, while the unemployment ranks and inflation grow.
Look at Quebec in September, 1977. The unemployment is 10.8 per cent. That was the official figure. Over 10 per cent unemployment! Newfoundland was 15.8 per cent, which is the adjusted figure. New Brunswick was 15.3 per cent. Nova Scotia was 10.4 per cent. Prince Edward Island was 9.3 per cent. All of eastern Canada had over 10 per cent unemployment. That has never happened before. If it happened during the depression, I did not know.
I should like to refer to youth unemployment. In Newfoundland, 22 per cent is the official figure referring to those under 25. In New Brunswick the figure is 19.8 per cent of those under 25. Saskatchewan is the lowest. It is 6.1 per cent. The real rate of unemployment in Newfoundland, according to our statisticians, is 26 per cent. That is the miserable state the country has been brought to by hon. gentlemen opposite. We are told that we should not be Cassandras, that we should not moan and groan, and that we should not complain because it is our own fault. That is what we have been told by the hon. members opposite. On March 11, 1972, the Prime Minister said that we could be obsessed by unemployment. You bet we can. We are obsessed by it.
Now the ministers are coming forth and blaming everyone but themselves. On September 13, for example, the Minister of Finance indicated that foreigners know that Canada is riding through the current world economic difficulties in comparatively high fashion, but Canadians do not have the same buoyancy, and instead we bitch. Are we wrong to complain? Are the hundreds of thousands of unemployed wrong? Are those laid off by INCO wrong? Are those laid off at Stephen-ville wrong? Are those laid off at St. Lawrence wrong? The Minister of Finance says that they are bitchers. The Prime Minister has said that the remedy is not to print money, but to work harder and to be more modest in our demands, in our

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
profits and in our wages. That was said by him on October 6. In other words; "Do what I say and not as I do".

speechtext: On October 11 in the Sunday Star the Prime Minister indicated that the answer is in ourselves. That has a faint literary ring. He also indicated that the answer is in self-discipline and the sense of values which we develop, that Canadians are a bit soft and have to be told they are soft. That is the kind of government we have. They blame everyone. They tell Canadians that they are soft. Yes, they are soft if they let the next election go by without turfing out the hon. members opposite.

Soft in the head. Because of the miserable amount of time we are given in this House to speak, I will refer only to one last quotation. It appeared last June in a newspaper article in British Columbia and reads in part as follows:
Kelowna-Iona Campagnolo, minister of state responsible for fitness and sport, says a federal election probably won't come before June of next year. ..
She also said unemployment and food prices will rise in Canada.
It was a positive promise that unemployment and food prices were going to rise in Canada. The article continues:
Canadians are going to have to understand that the fat times are over.
That is great advice. Yes, the fat times are over. Because of the hon. gentlemen opposite, their fat times are going to be positively concluded as soon as they have the courage to go to the people and put themselves to the test of the electorate.

There has been dismal failure in economic matters and in national unity matters. There has been complete, utter, and adject failure of government policy on the question of national unity and regional economic disparity. Nine years ago the government was going to eliminate, brutalize, terrorize, and absolutely stop regional economic disparity in Canada. Of course it has not, no matter what money is being spent.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and some of his Liberal colleagues went for a visit to the province of Newfoundland. They crawled across that province to tell us how good we had it. An article which appeared in The Evening Telegram dated September 13, 1977, reads as follows:
Regional economic expansion has generally failed in Newfoundland in terms of creating new secondary industries ...
It certainly has. The article continues:
Jamieson, who headed the department of regional economic expansion at one point in his political career, said that except for industries native to the region, industrial incentives have not "succeeded to a great extent" ...
Also the article indicates that there was not a complete failure by DREE because of infrastructure and so on. In other words, DREE is just a method of handing out moneys across

Canada to enable provinces to put in infrastructure. Good enough, but it is not overcoming regional economic disparity.
During the last nine years that the government has been in office, it has failed completely, utterly and absolutely. If it had any conscience at all, it would resign quietly. It should go to the electorate and ask the electorate if they want it to return to power. That would let someone else have a chance.

speechtext:
I am delighted to have been appointed critic of industry, trade and commerce. I will be able to have a few dialogues in the House this year with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). He was good enough to come to my nominating meeting just one year and one month ago in order to give me a good send off. Therefore I owe the hon. member something. Now he is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. That is important to Newfoundland, as well as the nation. I should like to give him a hint, that he must concentrate on fisheries and getting our fisheries products into the European Common Market and into countries other than the United States. That will be one of his priorities, if he does not want to have me after him constantly, both in and out of this House.
For the first time in 100 years we have a chance in Canada to break into the European market and markets other than the United States market. This must be one of the objectives of these negotiations which are now taking place under the so-called Tokyo Round. I hope he will not be as vague as he was on "Question Period" two weeks ago last Sunday. I have never heard anything as vague as some of the minister's references on that occasion. He has to do his homework, and I am prepared to wait another three or four days to see if he can be more specific. Also, he should be concerned about the travel deficit.
During last year Canadians travelling outside Canada spent $1.2 billion more than foreigners travelling in Canada. That huge deficit was a record for Canada up to that time. In the first six months of this year the deficit is $1.2 billion, and everyone is indicating that the deficit will be $2 billion by the end of the year, because of Canadians travelling abroad. 1 suppose that is because we are "fat cats", as the minister for sport and amateur fitness would say, or as the minister for amateur sport and fitness would say, or as the hon. fit minister would say. We are spending $2 billion more abroad than foreign tourists are spending here. That cannot continue.
The government has indicated that it is not going to put on mandatory controls. Therefore 1 suggest to the minister that one of his first jobs should be a "ban the tan" campaign. All of us have heard of the "ban the bomb" campaign. What we need is a "ban the tan" campaign. Every Canadian who dares to go south next winter and returns to Canada with a tan should be ostracized. That "ban the tan" campaign should be started now, and perhaps we will be able to reduce that $2 billion deficit next year. If hon. members get a tan from the lights in this Chamber, we can explain that.
October 25, 1977

I have one regret in connection with the Speech from the Throne. Her Majesty was here in Ottawa, we were all delighted to see her and, I guess, the nation was delighted to see her on television, apart from those who were invited by the government to Ottawa, and I will not go into that. My only regret is that Her Majesty's government sitting opposite refused to allow Her Majesty the Queen to visit parts of Canada other than the Ottawa area in 1977, in spite of invitations extended to her. In fact the advice that Her Majesty the Queen received from the government was not to visit the province of Newfoundland, as one example. A petition was signed by practically every member of the population as a declaration of loyalty, but it had to be sent over to London and delivered at Buckingham Palace by the daughter of one of the petitioners. Her Majesty did not come to Newfoundland because the Prime Minister would not advise her to do so. I hope that will not happen again. I hope that never again will the Queen's presence be reserved just for Ottawa and the people in the Ottawa region. 1 do not think that is right or proper.
The Kingston communique was mentioned by my colleague a few moments ago. It was put out by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and four premiers. We now have five Progressive Conservative premiers, half the country, and the Leader of the Opposition, which makes a country and a half, agreeing on what should be done. There are only two Liberal premiers left. The Prime Minister, who speaks for himself, and two premiers speak on those matters, and they scoff at what has happened at Kingston.
1 should like to speak on another subject for a moment. The government is giving advice to the people of Canada. It is telling them that they have to make some sacrifices, they have to produce and they have to lessen their demands, that a lot of what is happening is their fault, that we have to restrict our ability to get what we want, and so on. All this advice is coming to us. But when the people of Canada look at the government for inspiration, what do they see? They see, as our leader pointed out the other day, two cabinet ministers, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), whizzing out to Calgary in two separate jets, landing with their own separate parties, going to the same function, and then flying off again. That is the kind of sacrifice at which the public are looking. They are looking at raw politics in action.
There is supposed to be a great policy of relocating government departments and civil servants from Ottawa to places all around the country. Several weeks ago there was an announcement about relocating 2,500 civil servants and 15 agencies. Seven hundred and fifty people are supposed to go to Sherbrooke. So far as I know, every one of these moves was a move to a Liberal district, and most were removed to a district of a cabinet minister to try to prop them up in their feeble attempts to get elected next year.
The Hydrology Research Institute is supposed to move to Saskatoon. Well, the Minister of Transport may be suffering from water on the brain, but it is a pretty expensive way to get
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
at it to move the Hydrology Institute to examine him. The Farm Credit Corporation is moving to Camrose in Alberta, the constituency of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. If he were still on this side of the House what an outburst we would have heard from him if that move had taken place to the constituency of the Minister of Transport and not to his! That is what the public is seeing from this government which is asking for sacrifice and for restraint. What we are seeing is raw political chicanery in everything it does, from the Queen's visit to relocating civil servants.
One of the things we are wondering about in eastern Canada is that nothing seems to exist outside of central Canada. A happening in the last few days reinforces that impression, that is, the INCO close-downs at Sudbury and in other Ontario and Manitoba communities, resulting in the unemployment of over 3,000 people. It is very bad. But the fuss that is being made here in relation to these shut downs makes one wonder about the situation in eastern Canada. For example, 3,175 jobs will be lost in Ontario as a result of the INCO shut down, that is .078 per cent of the labour force of 4,048,000. Yet in Newfoundland six months ago the Labrador linerboard mill shut down on the west coast of Newfoundland and 1,500 people lost their jobs in the mill and out in the woods. In Newfoundland we have a labour force of 198,000. The loss of 1,500 jobs means that .76 per cent of the labour force became unemployed. Was there any outburst up here in central Canada, or any attention paid to it? No, hardly a twitter.
A mine is closing in St. Lawrence, Newfoundland, and 400 jobs will be lost. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did not even answer a letter from the Newfoundland government for two and a half months asking him to impose a tariff to save the mine, or to impose a quota. An oil refinery in Come-by-Chance is closing and over 600 jobs will be lost. Is there any fuss, any activity by the federal government to try to get it going again? No, none. All those close-downs will result in 2,500 jobs being lost, almost as many as here in Ontario, but they are being lost quietly despite our cries and our plaintive appeals, the appeals of a few members from that area, members from the west coast of Newfoundland.
The government was asked to assist the Newfoundland government to keep the Labrador linerboard mill going. The Newfoundland government could not keep it going any longer because of the huge expense and because it did not have the financial wherewithal, but the Government of Canada has done nothing in a substantial way to help that concern. In fact it has turned it down. Cabinet ministers say they are not in the business of saving jobs, they are in the business of creating jobs. Yet I look at the September 30 release by the minister's department and I see that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion are contributing SI 1.3 million to a firm called Valleyfield Chemical Products Limited to acquire and rehabilitate a CIL factory at Valleyfield to manufacture explosives, much of which is forgiveable and does not need to be paid back. Why is it being given? Because of this federal involvement, 250 jobs will be saved. That is what the release

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
says. So, to save 250 jobs in Quebec it is all right to lash out $11.3 million, but when you ask to help save 1,500 jobs in Stephenville, Newfoundland, you are laughed out of Ottawa. Let us call an election so we can show what we think of that in Newfoundland. This kind of inconsistency will be looked into a lot further before this session of parliament is over.
A civil war is going on between the Government of Canada and the government of Newfoundland. The government here is trying to crush the spirit of the government of Newfoundland. I have at least ten examples that I could give the House if I had the time to show what is happening there. Canada's representative, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is concerned about every country in the world except about the little province of Newfoundland which is being smothered and snuffled by him, by the government of which he forms a part.
A wood cutting project was suggested in connection with the Gull Island project in Labrador. Gull Island will be developed, if not next year, then in five or ten years. All that hydro power will not go to waste for ever; Canada needs it. The environmentalists have said that wood should be cut away on the sides of the lower Churchill river so that the reservoir will be in an area where all the wood has been cut out. The government of Newfoundland suggested to the government in Ottawa that it is a great work creation program which would involve employing some of the 900 loggers laid off at Labrador linerboard to start this wood cutting project on the reservoir. The project would take about four years and would employ about 400 loggers, and it would be worth while because the work has to be done anyway. The officials appeared to be delighted with this sensible suggestion for a make-work project. Yet the answer came months later from the minister of manpower and immigration, the now Minister of Employment (Mr. Cullen), that Canada Manpower cannot approve this proposal until it is certain that the project will proceed, the whole $2.5 billion project. They will wait until it is certain that it will proceed! What malarkey! It might be five years before this happens. That is their answer.
Ottawa must look at environmental considerations before giving the green light, and yet the environmentalists themselves have said that the wood must be cut off before the work is started. The member for the district says that no funding for this project will be considered until an environmental impact study has been done. I think we must do an impact study on this government and impact it right out of office.
Some hon. Mlembers: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
There is a fisheries confrontation. The government, through its Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc), is attempting to dominate and crush any plans, policies or suggestions for the development of the fisheries that the Newfoundland government has through its minister of fisheries. The Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry has examined this.
Newfoundland is the province most dependent on fisheries in the whole of the Dominion. Twenty-five per cent of our work force is in the fishery or connected with it, and 10 per

cent of our gross provincial product is involved in the fishery. It has great prospects for the future, yet when the provincial minister of fisheries sent a proposal to the federal government on May 11 outlining what should be done in various areas of the fishery it was repudiated without even the courtesy of a meeting. Most of the proposal was thrown out and the rest of it must wait until this government develops a policy for the Atlantic fishery. The federal minister refuses to meet with the provincial minister.
The Newfoundland government has started a program to build 100 longliners to replace vessels 40 to 65 feet long in the present fleet, but the 35 per cent subsidy that the federal government used to pay has been refused, and now the program will cost the Newfoundland government an additional $12 million. The federal government will not permit the chartering of foreign fishing vessels nor joint ventures.
I do not have time to go into details on all these matters, Mr. Speaker, but I submit that the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry should be permitted to examine the minister and his aides and to invite the minister from Newfoundland and his aides to appear before it to make recommendations in an effort to resolve this problem. That committee should show some guts, and the majority of its members should stop being slavish devotees of the government. This is an area where there is complete confrontation, but because of the British North America Act the federal minister can have the last word. He can have the last word while he is in office, but if he is not in office he can have no words at all. That is what will happen to the minister and this government if they do not adopt a better approach than this to the provinces.
1 have 100 examples, Mr. Speaker. There is the interprovincial ferry service, for instance. As a result of that service coming into operation, coastal boats no longer have to call at settlements, thus saving the Government of Canada great sums of money. The federal government agreed it would pay for the intra-provincial ferry services from certain islands to the mainland because it was saving money on the coastal boats. Now, however, the Minister of Transport tells the government of Newfoundland that it has to take over and pay for the ferry service. His list of crimes of omission and commission is long and I do not have time to deal with it properly.
The Cape Sambro is a trawler. This is the worst incident in recent months. There is a shipyard at Marystown, in the riding of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which is owned by the government of Newfoundland and employs at least 400 or 500 people. In the fall of 1975 the yard had no work and could not get work, so the government of Newfoundland decided to have a trawler built to the same specifications as earlier trawlers in the hope that someone would buy it- perhaps National Sea Products Ltd.-so that the yard could keep going. They spoke to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who told them that if they went ahead he could assure them they would get the 35 per cent subsidy, 22 per cent from the Department of Fisheries and 13 per cent from the Depart-
October 25, 1977

ment of Industry, Trade and Commerce, under regular programs. This was a $4,250,000 vessel so the subsidy was very important in order that the shipyard could compete with foreign yards.
The trawler was built and the minister was contacted about the subsidy in October, 1976, because officials in Ottawa were not talking much about it. There was an offer from National Sea Products Ltd. to buy the vessel for 10 per cent down with a 55 per cent mortgage, and the balance to be covered by the 35 per cent subsidy.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce agreed to pay the 13 per cent subsidy that goes to shipyards, but the Department of Fisheries has resolutely refused to pay the 22 per cent or $935,000, from that day to this. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is defying the Secretary of State for External Affairs saying that he will not pay the subsidy. The Secretary of State for External Affairs came to Newfoundland with his Liberal colleagues last September. He was questioned about this matter, and the following report appeared in the Evening Telegram of October 21:
The federal minister from Newfoundland said Sept. 22 the Cape Sambro affair had been a "foul up from day one" and, without making a specific commitment, said the federal government would do its best to straighten out the situation.
At his side, Fisheries Minister Romeo LeBlanc said on that occasion it is regrettable that the province went ahead and built the trawler on speculation that the full subsidy would be paid. He also said Ottawa would try to resolve matters.
He had better resolve them, Mr. Speaker. It was big of him to say it was regrettable they had gone ahead. They went ahead because his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, said they would get the subsidy. He said there had been a foul up and the federal government would do its best. Mr. Speaker, the best thing it can do is give the money, and if the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment does not, he will have to answer for it when he appears before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry. We will deal with him in the House and, as Churchill said, we will deal with him on the beaches and in the fields and in the sea and in the coves until he pays up that 22 per cent that his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, promised the poor little government of Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to say how pleased I was, and I know members of my constituency were as well, to have the Queen open our parliament recently. I was pleased and honoured to have the opportunity of meeting Her Majesty and His Royal Highness Prince Phillip. This was a great honour shared by many other members of parliament.
In keeping with tradition, 1 should like at this time to extend my congratulations to both the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood) on their thoughtful remarks which opened the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I should like to mention briefly the report submitted by the subcommittee on the the penitentiary system in Canada. I will not cover the background of the report because my colleague, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), spoke at some length last Friday about the recommendations made and their future implementation. As a member of that subcommittee I want to add that the report we produced was unanimous, representing all parties in the House of Commons. The feedback I have received from experts in the penal field and the general public has been positive and encouraging. The response of the minister, to date, has been reasonably supportive, and I hope that virtually all of the recommendations will be implemented and will receive the unanimous approval of the House.
At this time 1 wish also to thank my colleagues for their support and good wishes on my recent appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo).

I am not entering my new responsibilities empty handed, without experience, because I have been chairman of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs for the past three years. My duties there were made easier because of the active participation of all members and, as a result, good legislation was returned to the House for consideration and passage.
I want to mention one private member's bill which was dealt with by the committee, Bill C-221, introduced by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen), which proposed an amendment to the section of the Criminal Code

dealing with the abduction of a child. When parliament recessed, this bill was under consideration by the standing committee. I am confident that I have the full support of the House when 1 say that 1 hope that this bill will retain its present status so that the witnesses arranged can be heard and a report finalized in this forthcoming session.
When I was chairman of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs I followed with considerable interest and satisfaction the development of federal legislation on social services. As a matter of fact it was my pleasure to address a volunteer agency on the topic about this time last year. This is why I take particular pleasure today in speaking about the legislation which the government hopes to introduce in this session. For those hon. members who may not be aware of the development of this legislation 1 would like to take this opportunity to identify its origins and to suggest the form the legislation might take.
As a result of concerns being expressed by a growing number of Canadians, the federal and provincial ministers of welfare decided to have a look at our country's social security system. A social security review was launched soon after, with the release of the Working Paper on Social Security in Canada on April 18, 1973 by the then minister of national health and welfare, the present Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde).
As a direct result of this review there were a number of improvements in many areas. First, there were significant improvements in the old age security and guaranteed income supplement programs. Second, there were significant improvements in family allowance programs. Third, there was increased compatability between the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. Fourth, there was the introduction of indexing to federal income maintenance measures. Fifth, there was research into how the taxation system could be used to develop benefits for the working poor.
I now come to the developments with respect to social services which have occurred as a result of the review. I feel that the federal and provincial ministers have been particularly impressive in responding not only to the needs of the aged, the handicapped, and children, but also to the changing social climate between 1973 and today, a climate of increasing economic restraint and of changing concepts of confederation. 1 would like to discuss this climate a little more fully.
In the fall of 1974 one of the working parties which grew out of the review, the working party on social services, produced an interim report which contained a critical review of social services in Canada and proposed areas for further study and consideration. Following receipt of this report the then minister of national health and welfare proposed to his provincial colleagues federal sharing in a wider range of services than was possible under the Canada Assistance Plan and additional financing for improved services in the areas of rehabilitation services and support services for the aged and handicapped. In

May of 1975 the welfare ministers met and agreed to develop the necessary legislation in consultation with each other.
A year later, in June, 1976, general agreement was reached on an outline for the proposed legislation on social services. The federal government therefore began drafting the appropriate legislation, and consultation continued with respect to the regulations.
The proposed social services act, Bill C-57, was read for the first time in this House of June 20, 1977. Its presentation had been somewhat delayed by developments in the health sector. New legislation covering the federal contribution to Canada's health services took effect on April 1, 1977.
What is important to remember is that throughout the negotiations the provinces urged that the federal legislation on social services should allow them flexibility to develop services in response to their perceptions of their needs and priorities, provide them with security of financial arrangements, and avoid undue administrative complexity.
As the development of the legislation and the negotiations with the provinces on the regulations progressed, it became apparent that the conditional cost-sharing approach might no longer be the most appropriate instrument to promote the improvement of social services and to provide the provinces with the flexibility they desired. There has been a growing concern that the legislation as proposed might be difficult to administer. It was feared that the introduction of block financing for health services in April, 1977, would make administrative matters even more complex because of the close relationship between many of the services, such as homemakers' services and nursing services.
Furthermore, the trend in an increasing number of provinces was to integrate health and welfare services, thus making less clear the line between them and making certain service definitions difficult to evolve. Too much complexity in a federal-provincial agreement would mitigate against positive working relationships between the two levels of government, and in terms of federal-provincial relations this was an important consideration. However, it was equally important in terms of the development of the sector and the improvement of social services in Canada.
The federal government has responded vigorously and creatively to these concerns. The former minister of national health and welfare made an alternative offer to the provinces which, if accepted, would provide them with the basic financial security they desire, while at the same time allowing them maximum flexibility and minimum administrative complexity.
In September of this year the minister proposed to the provinces that a block financing arrangement be substituted for the conditional shared cost approach which was reflected in Bill C-57. Under a block financing approach the federal contribution in 1978-79 and onward would be based on a per capita formula rather than on provincial expenditures.
The formula provides for expansion and growth in the sector, recognizes price changes, and includes a levelling factor which would bring all provinces to the same per capita pay-
October 25, 1977

ment in ten years' time. The combination of these factors would have the effect of raising the federal per capita contribution of $22 in 1977-78 to close to $70 per capita in 1987-88, given current projections of the rate of growth. The federal contribution in a first full year of operation would be some $700 million.
I would like to emphasize three very important points. Some comments have been made, in the news media and elsewhere, that the federal government's offer to block finance the social services represents a withdrawal from the sector. Nothing could be further from the truth. The government attaches just as much importance to the development of social services as it did when it introduced Bill C-57. Indeed, it has demonstrated that commitment by including in the offer $132 million as its share of the growth and expansion that are necessary in the field of social services.
I would like to emphasize that the block financing arrangement would cover precisely those services which were defined in the social services bill tabled in this House on July 20, 1977.
I should stress that I am referring here only to social services and not to the income maintenance needs of disadvantaged Canadians. Those needs will continue to be met through a variety of federal programs and through the income maintenance provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan.
It is still too early to determine what the reaction of the provinces to this imaginative proposal will be, and hence to predict when new legislation reflecting it will be ready for presentation to the House. The Minister of National Health and Welfare very recently wrote to her colleagues and hopes to have their views on this matter in the near future. If the response continues to be as positive as has been evidenced so far, the government will introduce a revised social services bill during this session.
I know of no real reason why the over-all response to this attractive offer should be anything but positive. On the one hand, the governments of the provinces would be completely free to respond to the needs in their provinces in accordance with their own priorities. On the other hand, both levels of government would have their energies freed to work together on social policy issues rather than having to maintain detailed administrative arrangements, with the attendant friction.
In responding as positively as it has to provincial concerns I believe that the federal government is laying the groundwork for an excellent model of co-operation with the provinces which will lead to greater social progress in Canada in a way more in keeping with our developing confederation.
I would now like to direct my comments to our economic policy. In the past year the government has published two discussion papers. The first was "The Way Ahead" and the second "An Agenda for Co-operation". Both papers suggest that it is necessary to find a better way of managing our economy, a more equitable method to spread out the wealth when times are good, and an improved way of pulling together when times are bad. The Speech from the Throne, the address by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the economic and fiscal statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) all
The Address-Mr. Robinson
echoed a similar theme regarding our present economic state: high inflation, slow growth, and high unemployment. To quote the Prime Minister, "We were in a true sense, a nation living beyond our means."
The Minister of Finance outlined some of the measures that the government will take to improve our present economic climate. I would like to discuss only a few, controls, further job creation programs, and the encouragement to the business sector.
It is two years since the establishment of the Anti-Inflation Board. Controls have helped greatly to check the inflationary spiral. During that period the Board has operated just about on target. Costs have been brought down, wage settlements are down, and the consumer price index has been brought down as well. You will realize that the government does not want to intervene indefinitely. Therefore the Minister of Finance announced that a phase-out of controls will begin on April 14, 1978. The Anti-Inflation Act will be amended, and an agency will be established to monitor price and cost developments.
Many groups have called for the immediate end to controls, but they do not seem to realize that their solution would only result in a rapid escalation of wages and prices, which would feed inflation and which would do nothing toward stimulating the economy or reducing unemployment. This gradual phaseout will allow us to sustain fiscal and monetary restraint.
There is no question that the Canadian economy is facing a very serious unemployment problem. The labour force has grown rapidly, with an especially high influx of young people into the labour market. Youth unemployment is a world-wide phenomenon and Canada has been a leader in providing innovative direct employment programs, the most recent being Canada Works and Young Canada Works. Four hundred and fifty million dollars have been already budgeted for these and other programs. The Minister of Finance informed us that an additional allocation of $150 million would be made available to create work projects in high unemployment areas. It was also stated that the government was exploring a new approach to job creation schemes in the form of a new program of employment credit for private business firms.
I fully support these new measures. However, I am keenly aware that these programs do not provide long term employment. We must look to private enterprise to supply this employment. However, job growth will only result if our industries are capable of better productivity so that they can actively compete in the world market place. There is strong international competition for productive resources and markets.
During the last session the government took several initiatives to assist Canadian business. For example, the Enterprise Canada 77 program is an effort to enhance development in the business community. At this time, all across the country, businessmen are being invited to attend seminars and workshops on export financing, technological innovation, and productivity, to name a few. The Minister of Finance stated that

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. La Salle
the fiscal measures mentioned in the March budget would be reintroduced. These include the introduction of a 3 per cent inventory allowance, the enrichment of the dividend tax credit, and the extension of the investment tax credit.
It is important to note that we have recognized the need for, and are prepared to participate in further consultation and co-operation with the provinces and labour and business, if our industrial sector is to get back on its feet and create the much needed employment for Canadians.
For the last few minutes I have been speaking about what policies the government has taken and will adopt to revitalize the Canadian economy, but at this point I would like to turn the tables, using the Kennedy approach, and ask all Canadians if they are prepared to contribute. To quote the Prime Minister:
What is needed is a simple decision on the part of the Canadian people to co-operate to keep their costs down, to live within their means, to act together in a spirit of co-operation in every area of the economy.
Aside from our preoccupation with the economic concerns of this country, Canadians are individually and collectively reaching out to discover what links us together as a Canadian people and by what means we can express our dedication to the Canadian spirit. With the passage of bill 101 by the National Assembly of Quebec, the national unity debate has intensified. No longer do some of us underestimate the dedication of the Parti Quebecois government, a government which sincerely believes that separation is the only way in which the French culture and language can survive.
All Canadians, French and English alike, are at the crossroads. A choice must be made. Some consensus must emerge on the future of our country. Therefore I was pleased when the Prime Minister announced that during this session legislation would be introduced concerning a referendum, which will allow the federal government to consult with all Canadians on the national unity issue.
The Speech from the Throne reiterates the Prime Minister's wish that we participate more actively in the reshaping of the future of Canada, and to quote from the Speech from the Throne:
The government dedicates itself profoundly to the rediscovery of the spirit of unity. It wishes to learn from all who are interested in Canada and who have thoughts on how it can be a better place in which to live.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this long traditional debate. First, like previous speakers, I would like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the motion on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I admit that perhaps I would not have been as generous as they were in their comments on the throne speech, but anyway they are two new members to whom 1 would like to wish much success in the interests of their own electors.
I would also like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that I represent a constituency which as most others in Canada is now experiencing the problems and concerns stated in the throne

speech. I also come from a particularly tormented province taking into account the political and economic circumstances. My constituency as many others needs a certain economic impetus. Agriculture is also having some difficulties. The unemployment rate is unacceptable and I think that I am only representing a constituency which is not unlike many others. During the next few weeks, no doubt I will have the opportunity to deal with some projects or pieces of legislation that could solve these difficulties. I also hope to have the opportunity to make some comments that will be taken into good consideration by hon. members on the government side.
I listened very carefully to the Speech from the Throne and also with interest to speeches delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). I draw from them all a very clear conclusion: the obvious recognition of a difficult if not catastrophic situation at both the economic and political levels. Of course both speakers called for co-operation from all Canadians to redress the present situation. Both recognized the absolute need to obtain the confidence of the Canadian people, thus inviting as well the official opposition to co-operate with them to help regain this confidence. In ten years, I have never seen a government as ill at ease, as concerned about the various problems as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, can anyone believe that, as members of the official opposition who have the responsibility and duty to denounce, on behalf of the Canadian people and with all our might, the failure of the current administration, we could co-operate with this government and help it obtain this trust? What do they take us for, Mr. Speaker? Could we ask the Canadian people to trust a government which has demonstrated such evident inaction, which has failed to achieve the objectives it had set for itself in 1968, from the "just society" to national unity, which was responsible again quite recently for the elimination of some 6,000 dairy producers in the province of Quebec alone, which had succeeded in fostering so much hope, then creating so many needs which finally turned into so many cruel disappointments.
But then 1 say they are expecting too much from us, much too much indeed. Mr. Speaker, I would like to give a fairly faithful and precise account of the specific reasons why we, members of the official opposition, felt we had to decline an invitation by the minister although he claimed he needed that kind of confidence. Should we remind him of the situation we are facing now? I suppose the Speech from the Throne overlooked this matter of equal opportunities and economic justice, of difficulties and cultural injustice in the future. In my opinion, the Speech from the Throne should have been read five years ago. In my view we are in a slump, therefore, we cannot possibly ask the Canadian people to trust the Speech from the Throne.
I would like to give a few examples to support my statements which are very harsh indeed, Mr. Speaker. When Canada celebrated its centennial in 1967, it was one of the
October 25, 1977

privileged countries in the world. We were a simple, vigorous and flourishing country which could look confidently towards its future. It was a country where, in spite of different origins, languages and cultures, people were showing signs of good will and were ready to make the necessary compromises to live together in some kind of satisfactory cohabitation, so that in spite of the normal frictions and necessary adjustments we were moving slowly but steadily towards a mode of mutual tolerance and harmony. In a word, Canada was moving forward and it was possible to believe that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right when he said that the twentieth century belonged to Canada.
Ten years have passed and all this is disappearing and will soon be nothing but a memory. Ten years later, we find ourselves in a country stuck in alarming economic programs which are about to paralyze for a long time our economic growth and development, a country divided by political and linguistic prejudices, a country which is wondering about its future. What has happened in this ten-year period to make the butterfly turn into a caterpillar and the dream become a nightmare? In 1968, Mr. Speaker, after the Centennial celebrations, a general election put at the head of the government a man who, we must admit, hoisted himself by the sheer power of his personality and intelligence. So deep has been his influence on the economy and even our national fabric that he unknowingly has confused and cast them adrift. I know that government members will accuse me of petty partisanship because I am attacking their party leader. True, he is a personality above average, but, personally, I am not so blind as to be unable to see him as he actually is.
I am taking the Prime Minister and this government to task all the more easily. I know they are able to defend themselves. I also know that he is a Quebecker just like me and that the words "franfais" and "franchise" have the same root. Whether members opposite admit it or not, I say that the frustrations and difficulties which our country is now experiencing stem from the personality and the behaviour of this government and of the man who has managed the affairs of Canada for nearly a decade, Mr. Speaker.
It has been said that the Prime Minister has charisma, that he exudes an uncommon magnetism; it is true. But it is also true that he flaunts his arrogance, that he knows nothing about flexibility and that he does not recognize his errors readily. It is also said that the Prime Minister is an intellectual, that he is refined, that he is quick-witted, which is also true. But it is equally true that his line of reasoning is often a one-way street, that he plays with words like a juggler, and that he is slow in adapting to new realities. Besides, the Prime Minister himself has in the past said of himself that he constantly sought out new challenges, that he found it difficult to conform, that he loved a tough fight, that he did not care about details, and very little about whether or not people agreed with him. All those aspects of his character, Mr. Speaker, combine to throw light on the ever astonishing performance of the Prime Minister since 1968, in this House as well as outside.
The Address-Mr. La Salle
I wanted to draw that rough sketch of what I believe to be his qualities and his faults, for I feel that therein lies the true explanation for his actions since he has come to power, actions which are but the prelude to the economic and political stagnation in which we now find ourselves.
In his speech last week, the Prime Minister decided at long last to recognize that the country is up against serious economic problems, but again he would have us believe that it all happened as if by magic, because of the economic situation throughout the world, because of inflation, because of unemployment, because Canadians live beyond their means; in short, because of everything save him and his government.
But he took good care not to admit that for the past nine years he had tried to pass as an economist without any qualifications in that field. Nor did he admit that his own views on the most effective ways to fight unemployment and inflation had swayed the Cabinet into adopting short term policies over the past few years, which failed to get to the roots of the problem. Incidently, I would be curious to know the views of the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner on the economic philosophy of the present prime minister. The Prime Minister would not confess that he had made a mistake on the issue of price and wage controls. He scorned my party's suggestions during the 1974 electoral campaign but ended up by having to implement them a year and a half after. The difference is that they were 18 months overdue and were applied without previous consultation with those affected by these measures. And as a matter of fact these controls proved almost ineffective because business and labour were not involved in their application.
Finally, the Prime Minister does not really know how to remove the controls because of the climate of mistrust and uncertainty he created by his attitude in the economic world. Such was the disastrous economic performance of this government for almost 10 years. And it is that same government and that same man who spoke about leadership during the 1974 campaign. In 1972, he had another slogan: This nation is strong, he proclaimed everywhere. Indeed, the country was strong, but he succeeded in breaking it up.
However, the most disappointing performance of the government leader concerns national unity. Our great expert on constitutional matters has done so much that the cannons on the Plains of Abraham are perking up.
Never had separatism been so strong before the advent of this government in 1968. But I suggest that it is himself and his government that are responsible for the rise of separatism in Quebec, because of their arrogance and rigidity, their continuing reliance on the status quo, their obvious contempt for provincial grievances and their morbid fear of giving up the least bit of federal authority. Indeed, he is the man responsible for the rise of separatism in Quebec.
Today, he would have us believe that the separatist thesis and the coming into power of the Parti Quebecois on November 15 are at the root of all the ills suffered by our country at present. But he fails to say that he is responsible for the rigid, insensitive and costly implementation of the Official Lan-

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. La Salle
guages Act which only succeeded in upsetting the Englishspeaking provinces without meeting the aspirations of the province of Quebec that were quite different, Mr. Speaker.
Because he had promised English Canada that his bilingualism policy would deal with the problem of national unity-and he still maintains this-the Prime Minister raised great hopes that were frustrated. Because he always persisted in reducing the constitutional problem to a mere linguistic dimension, he only succeeded in aggravating the grievances of Quebec towards the federalist system.
In addition, how is it that over those years, the Prime Minister has never heeded the growing menace of separatism and did not see fit to warn English Canada about it.
I shall quote his own words to back my contention that either he has very little political foresight, or he was deliberately hiding the truth.
Mr. Speaker, as I have several very interesting quotations to jmake this evening, may I call it six o'clock, and continue my remarks at eight o'clock?

So I shall continue, Mr. Speaker. Before we adjourned, I was saying that along with my comments, 1 would make a few quotations to illustrate the total unawareness of the Prime Minister, as shown by some statements he made over a number of years.
For instance, in May 1966, he said it was unlikely that Quebec would ever want to separate. In May 1968, he asserted that federalism was gaining ground in the province of Quebec. In January 1970, he said that federalism was not threatened. In July 1971, he contended that his firm stand on the constitutional issue had prevented separatism from developing in Quebec during the past three years. In September 1972, he claimed that as a result of the efforts made by his government, Canadians had never been so united. In October 1972, he predicted that separatism was disappearing in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, those are the statements made by the Prime Minister throughout Canada and in particular in other provinces than Quebec. On top of that, a few months before November 15 of last year, he announced to the Canadian people, and this beats all: Separatism is dead. However, he said, one should not lose all hope since last January, he came back again saying: Separation will not take place. Let us hope for the sake of this country that this time he will be right. But it is above all in his discussions with provincial governments that one can see how great are his diplomatic skill and statesmanship.

In May 1967, he denounces the aggressiveness of provincial premiers. In January 1968, he states that it is time to engage in a fight against the provinces about the constitutional reform. In January 1968, as well, one week before the constitutional conference, he warns Quebec that it empire building is out of the question. In March 1968, he accuses Premier Johnson of negotiating in bad faith. Also in March 1968, he says that the Quebec government is "an insignificant provincial government". In April 1969, he says about Premier Bertrand that he has lost his senses. In April 1970, he describes the Quebec premier as an unimportant provincial politician. In May 1970, he accuses the provincial premiers of blackmail. In February 1972, he accused the British Columbia premier of being narrow-minded. In June 1972, he also called Quebec's claims insignificant. Finally, more recently he derided former Premier Bourassa-one of his cousins-for eating hot dogs.
As you see, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the government did not spare any efforts to bring about national harmony in this country. If only the Prime Minister would remember a statement he made in 1971. I don't know if my friends opposite remember. He said he would resign if a separatist government were ever elected in Quebec. You will not mind, Mr. Speaker, if I deplore aloud that certain promises prove to be empty words.
From the beginning of my speech I have tried to establish the link between the man who has been running this country for nearly ten years and the dramatic imprint he has left on it. He is, of course, a man out of the ordinary, I admit without hesitation. How could he be otherwise and yet manage to stay in power in spite of so many contradictions, disappointments, mistakes and turnabouts? He has been unique in many respects and it will be said of him that he was not a prime minister exactly like the others. But legend lasts only so long and with the coming winter I find comfort along with a very large number of my fellow citizens in the thought that spring will finally bring the final curtain down on a show that has already lasted for too long. Quite fortunately for the future of Canada, I think we have started the final act entitled: The colossus with clay feet. Mr. Speaker, those statements made across this country knowingly or unknowingly hid the truth. Only the Prime Minister can tell for sure. I made reference to a series of statements which were misinformation spread across Canada. Mr. Speaker, I think that those quotations were correctly interpreted. After reassuring English Canada particularly that separatism will decrease in the province of Quebec, they had the gall to support the CBC when it misrepresented the facts throughout the country. 1 say to all Canadians, Mr. Speaker, it would have been wiser to reflect on the CBC broadcasts instead of believing the Prime Minister's statements, and this, for the last four or five years.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to remind you, when I say that the separatism issue in the province of Quebec is due to the inflexibility of this government, I would like to remind you also of those negative answers made not only to the present first minister but also to Mr. Bourassa, Mr. Bertrand, Mr. October 25, 1977

Johnson, Mr. L'Allier, Mr. Elardy, Mr. St-Pierre, who relied on a great number of members from Quebec in Ottawa, on representations which fell on deaf ears, and which were so many reasons they gave at that time to the present first minister to reject a federalism that they wished and still wish to be viable.
With regard to the representations made by the province of Quebec particularly, could the government remember also the common front put up by the finance ministers against the federal government and realize that the views of the province of Quebec were also shared by the nine other provinces in some respects. And now, a few days ago, the Prime Minister laughed at us when he said that no government has ever been as flexible as his. But, Mr. Speaker, a few provincial Liberals remember that the measures advocated by this government led to disaster in the last provincial election.
The dairy policy which deprived Mr. Bourassa of invaluable support because of the mismanagement of an ill-conceived, ill-prepared federal policy proved very costly to the Quebec milk producers. I could mention the Ontario milk producers because that issue has not been settled, but 1 will come back to that. Mr. Speaker, for ten long years we have listened to those men, and I say again that they have the gall to ask for our cooperation, to win the public confidence. But the only way to settle that question is not through a cabinet shuffle which will not produce any new ideas due to the absence of new faces.
Mr. Speaker, I remember that it was rumoured at the time of the by-election that the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Lamontagne) had been promised a portfolio in the forthcoming cabinet shuffle. I realize that he must be disappointed, I am sorry he is absent from the House, and I suggest he could have brought something new to this 10-year old government. The ministers have played some sort of musical chairs; the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was shouting from the top of his lungs last Thursday that the worst thing was the fear of fear itself, not realizing that he was shaking all over as he was saying this. We are not to expect any new idea from this cabinet, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance has been there, with all his colleagues, for the past 10 years and he was supposed to come up with new ideas. What did we get? Leftovers. The government has clearly demonstrated that it is exhausted and the only solution is to get rid of it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bonaven-ture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) is asking me if 1 am kidding, after this huge failure of some 10-year duration in the area of unemployment. Huge failure also in the area of national unity, under a government which still claims to be the government of the people, even after the elections of a separatist party in Quebec.
Furthermore this same government, elected in Quebec, promised ten years ago to achieve Canadian unity. Is it not a colossal failure, Mr. Speaker? And do you suppose that we, the members from Quebec, are going to co-operate with this government in an effort to convince the Canadian people to
The Address-Mr. La Salle
back it up? The Canadian population would resent it, Mr. Speaker. They have shown unparalleled incompetence. And as far as the economy is concerned, to this day this government has shown complete lack of competence and effectiveness; for how long has this been going on?
I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) boast about the tax reduction when we know that our leader and our financial critic have been asking for this reduction for the past two years in order to give a minimum purchasing power to Canadians in view of the absence of positive action and new initiatives. Are we going to support this government, Mr. Speaker? No, we are not and we shall do everything in our power to remind the Canadian people of its colossal failure at the political and economic levels.
In Washington recently, the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine certainly heard his beloved leader express his wish to make an in-depth re-evaluation of our constitution and say the exact opposite of what he has been doing for the past ten years. Suddenly, the truth has to come out. Recently in this House he gave us a lecture on history. Canadians know it and Quebecers think that they do too. Mr. Speaker, I believe that because of our responsibilities as members of parliament, we must denounce the stand-patitis of this government and refuse to help it regain the confidence of the people when this government has continually favoured confrontation among unions, businessmen and provinces at a time when it would have been essential to bring all these people together for a round table discussion!
It is unthinkable to try to restore our economic climate without those people, and on this level also, the government is doing nothing. And we know that it needs now the co-operation and the advice of these businessmen. We have been asking for a long time that the government meet with these associations to try to find a way to restore the economic climate, and now of course, there will be the question of a referendum, which is another original idea of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and this government to hide the real problems. They are not afraid of increasing the tensions which exist in Canada by using the referendum issue in order to conceal the real problems. These problems have been concealed under the bilingualism issue. As this may show a lack of initiative or imagination, they are coming up with the referendum formula. But this is not what we need. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the important thing is to prove not only to Quebec but to all the provinces that there is a possibility of restoring the economic climate, thereby enabling the Canadian people, both English and French, to fraternize just like they did ten years ago during the centennial celebrations. This is the way to proceed.
When Canadians are made to believe that the solution lies in national unity, this is not true; this is a smokescreen. It is by restoring the economic climate, by establishing a minimum income for each citizen that we will be able to get Quebec and all the provinces around the same table and I would be very pleased to accept this challenge. We now have the proof of the tremendous failure of this government. We, in the opposition, cannot believe for a single moment in the projections made by
