Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to straighten the facts which were so twisted by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle).
For instance, when he says that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) refuses a third option for Canada, the hon. member for Joliette knows that he is not telling the truth since the Prime Minister has never said that in his speech to this House. On the contrary, he did say that he rejects the option of sovereignty association but not a third option.
To start with, Mr. Speaker, if hon. members would permit me I would like to express my respect and admiration for our graceful Queen Elizabeth II on the occasion of her Silver Jubilee, and to convey to Her Majesty as well as to His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh, my appreciation for their presence which greatly enhanced the brilliance of these celebrations in Canada.
I also wish to congratulate the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, my hon. colleagues from Louis-Hebert and Malpeque (Messrs. Dawson and Wood) for the admirable way in which they discharged their duties.
Mr. Speaker, to some people who are usually found in the opposition, the speech delivered by Her Majesty at the opening of this session offers nothing or next to nothing which might relieve the hardships which Canada is now experiencing. For anyone however who takes the trouble to carefully reread that important document, for instance if the hon. member for Joliette had bothered to read carefully the Speech from the Throne, we would not have had to listen, this afternoon before dinner and since eight o'clock, to the poppycock he has so generously delivered to this House. Any person who reads that speech carefully, Mr. Speaker, will see a large number of measures which prove how serious the government's intents are to alleviate, if not completely resolve our economic problems and one must admit, whatever the hon. member for Joliette may think and say, that since last November 15, with the coming to power in the province of Quebec of the PQ government which is determined to break up this country.
80025-18'/2

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. Bechard
The most important measures of the legislative program mentioned in the Speech from the Throne and on which I would like to briefly comment in the time allotted to me under our rules are as follows: Those dealing with economic development, particularly in areas where unemployment is at the highest level, the overhauling of our national transportation system and the issue of Canadian unity.
As far as the economy is concerned, the measures presented to us in the Speech from the Throne and which become clearer as ministers take part in this debate and as this session unfolds, if implemented without too much delay and used wisely by manufacturers and Canadians at large to their advantage in the same spirit that motivated those who drafted them, namely the government, these measures alone, I repeat, should make our national economy healthy again as it has been especially since the last world war.
As representative of an area quite remote from large centres of the country with a relatively small population, I can say that its economic development has not kept pace with that of more favoured areas of this country. Our geographical location still offers a climate which is similar to that of many other more prosperous places in Quebec and in other Canadian provinces. It also has access to the St. Lawrence River, the cheapest means of transportation available and its scenic sites attract thousands of tourists every year. Furthermore its manpower, if given a chance, is characterized by its adaptability to all modern technological changes. Our geographical location as we have always been told is the major handicap to our economic take-off.
Our main natural resources are forest products, fisheries, agriculture, tourism and for the past few years, mining. These are, Mr. Speaker, the five economic sectors from which all the people in my riding directly or indirectly live off. Some commendable efforts have been made in the past few years- this must frankly be admitted, in spite of the objections of my colleague from Joliette-by successive Liberal governments in Ottawa and since the beginning of the 1960's to strengthen the economy of our area including my constituency of Bonaven-ture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine.
For example, in the forestry field, to the important sawmills of the Madawaska Corporation Limited, now the Lacroix Lumber Limited of Carleton, Nouvelle and Causapscal has been added a new pulp and paper mill in New Richmond and this through the policies initiated by the Pearson government, in the form of a tax allowance under regional development to create employment. Let us also point out the policy of land consolidation, more generous subsidies to milk producers, the increased development of tourism, the adequate development of fishing ports at designated places, subsidies for the establishment of various small plants or the improvement of existing ones, subsidies to fishermen and fish producers, increased activity in construction and establishment in our area of the sacrosanct Housing and Mortgage Corporation which up to 1962 was almost totally unknown to us, federal contribution to the improvement of our highway system within the federal-provincial program for the development of Eastern Quebec
(Mr. Bdchard]
and special programs for the creation of jobs: LIP, Canada Works, now Opportunities for Youth Program, manpower mobility program, on-the-job training program, etc.
But since our regional economy had been lagging so far behind, much remains to be done to bring it up to standards. Our people, specially our youths, are leaving gradually for lack of adequate jobs. We must try and free them from their ever present concerns over the spectre of having to depend in such large numbers upon society as a whole, to rely on welfare or too often on unemployment insurance.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, the March budget made me particularly happy, because it increased by 10 per cent the investment tax credit in my area so as to reflect the government's determination to support industrial development and create jobs. I am even happier now since the government announced in the Speech from the Throne that tax reductions will be reinforced to stimulate our economy. I feel the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and his colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) should concentrate their efforts on ways to promote greater productivity, to encourage our small and average businesses through fiscal measures and credit facilities more in keeping with their ability to pay and with conditions more acceptable and more suitable to their type of business.
For instance, we should not penalize the borrower who would reimburse the government or the Federal Business Development Bank before the expiry date. The state should not act as a banker or a money lender to gain benefits or make money. If a businessman or a merchant who borrowed from the Federal Business Development Bank or from some other federal agency is so successful in his business because of that government policy which enables him to repay ahead of time, so much the better for him. This would free funds from which a larger number of small businesses might benefit. Let us relieve them from the petty annoyances of stacks and stacks of paper work such as countless and complicated daily, weekly, monthly, yearly reports and so on.
One businessman in the Magdalen Islands told me recently that one of his employees works only one hour a week for him, spending the rest of her time working for the state to file weekly reports which must be made according to federal or provincial legislation. The individual, the small businessman is therefore an asset to the state, for he must hire and pay an employee to fill in the reports which should be done by a civil servant of the state. The only hour during which that employee who is paid by her employer actually works for him is when she prepares the payroll at the end of the week.
The Speech from the Throne gives us an idea of the government's optimism concerning the benefits which Canada should gain from the multilateral trade negotiations which are taking place in Geneva. I sincerely believe that the future will prove it right. For it is imperative, Mr. Speaker, if we want to keep our traditional industries which generate a great many jobs, such as the textile and shoe industries, industries which
October 25, 1977

are already facing great difficulties, that special efforts be made to make them more competitive than they really are just now. In this respect, my own province of Quebec is seriously affected. The pulp and paper industry is facing enormous difficulties and the province of Quebec, in view of the extent of its forest, is again greatly affected. Under the present conditions, the competition of the United States, which depends on various factors, is almost impossible to meet, partly because of their advanced technology, a climate which is more conducive to a quicker growth, and the cost of rail transportation which is notably too high in Canada.
It is consequential then that I should deal with transportation in Canada and particularly in my area. I could say the same about the whole of Eastern Canada, since the Speech from the Throne indicates without any of the details which will become known later on that several measures will be introduced during this session with a view to improving our national transportation system. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that it will not be too soon nor will it be a luxury! Members of the House of Commons have heard me plead rather regularly and often with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) or the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) to improve rail, air, sea and even road transportation in Eastern Canada so that 1 do not have to remind you that everything is not working smoothly in that area, particularly in my area.
As far as air transportation is concerned, not to mention the Magdalen Islands or other places, improvements have been required for more than ten years and they are long in being brought about. This means of transportation is so to speak almost non existent on a regular basis in Bonaventure. It seems however that the problem, as far as the Magdalen Islands are concerned, is about to come to a happy ending. I shall therefore refrain from dwelling further on the matter, reserving my comments for some later date, if need be. But, in the part of my riding located on the mainland, the situation is a disaster. Though the Minister of Transport and his officials are aware that there is at Bonaventure a landing strip of some 6,000 feet completely paved and lighted, with possibilities for an extension if warranted, there are hesitations, delays, regrettably, I would even say tragically, about the Gaspe airport as a regional airport, while the DOT experts have said repeatedly that it is impossible to equip it with air traffic instruments (ILS) because of the neighbouring mountains.
Improvements to the islands' airport have been delayed by the difficulties encountered at Gaspe, because, in addition, Quebecair demands the simultaneous development of those two airports. By virtue of what authority are those views now being imposed upon the DOT? The Bonaventure airport, which belongs to the Quebec government, it is true, lends itself magnificently to the improvements that would make of it an all-weather airport where aircraft of all sizes and power could land without any problem. All the government need do is to start negotiations with the authorities of the province of Quebec and obtain its agreement to setting up in that part of the Gaspe peninsula a regional airport from which an airline located in the Magdalen Islands could link the south-east coast
The Address-Mr. Bechard
of Gaspe, Bonaventure, and the islands directly to Quebec and Montreal.
That suggestion, which I have already made to the department, would take away nothing from Gaspe; it would naturally keep its existing airport which in turn could easily be linked with the regional airport at Bonaventure. That solution, Mr. Speaker, would, in the final analysis, be far more logical than that which is being suggested to us by asking the people of Bonaventure, which is located further west, and who want to go even further west, to Quebec, Montreal and elsewhere, to go board the plane at Gaspe, fly some 125, 150 or 175 miles further east, and then come back towards the west. Why, I wonder, can we not use what already exists before thinking of investing millions of dollars in relocating an airport that has already cost several million dollars?
Now, let us consider rail transportation.
In our area as well as in many others in this country, the railway is the most reliable and economical means of transportation and for us, in the Gaspe peninsula, it is the only means of transport we can now rely on. However, as I already said elsewhere, the negligence of the CNR in the field of passenger service, and I apologize to the man who is sitting in the Chair, a former railway employee, their failure to modernize their equipment and their passenger services, for example, has lead to such a disruption of our railway system that unfortunately the people are turning instead to the bus service which is not a very good alternative on long routes such as Gaspe-Montreal.
And now the CNR has asked the Canadian Transport Commission to abandon the passenger service, the only one we have in the Gaspe peninsula, between Matapedia and Gaspe. I had the opportunity to state my objections before the Transport Commission which held public hearings in Gaspe recently, particularly in my constituency, on my behalf and on behalf of my constituents, at this request of the CNR, and to make a number of suggestions. Therefore I shall not repeat the arguments I put forward on that occasion. I shall simply ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the government to categorically and unequivocally turn down that irresponsible and, moreover, unfair request of the CNR.
Our railway companies anxious as they are to make a profit, and to that end to get rid of passenger service, in my opinion and in that of several of my voters and several Canadians, are charging excessive rates, which places our industrialists and businessmen and the products they manufacture in an unfavourable situation in relation to their U.S. competitors, for example. A good example is that of pulp and paper mills which are not only unable to compete in terms of labour costs but are also at a disadvantage with regard to transportation costs. I hope that among the many measures proposed in the Speech from the Throne and aimed at improving Canada's national transportation system, there will be some to correct those anomalies.
I also want to take this opportunity to say that I am dead set against the policy of the Minister of Transport, not the depart-

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. Bechard
ment's, but of the minister who wants the user, in this area of transportation, to pay for the services he obtains, as if he did not, through taxes or transportation rates between Montreal and the Magdalen Islands. Such a policy is perhaps fine for the director of a private company, but when it comes to Crown corporations in a country as vast as ours where transportation costs among other things greatly affect the cost of our manufactured products, and thus the competitiveness of our products on foreign markets, it is not realistic to want to implement such a policy in Canada. Our remote areas will never be able to survive and prosper.
The people in this country are ready to pay for these services and they are already paying a good price, but to add to their burden would be to condemn them to perpetual stagnation. That is why they are prepared to pay directly, but they ask all better off Canadians to help them through the tax system, as has been the case and as is still the case today. If the minister persists in implementing that policy, ferry, air and railway transportation, and consequently the whole economy of our areas, of my area in particular, instead of making progress will decline, including all sectors-forestry, agriculture, fisheries, mining, tourism, and so on.
The measures proposed in the Speech from the Throne, if they are implemented immediately and with good judgment, understanding and consideration for remote areas, will restore the confidence that one can feel is at least shaky in the whole Canadian economic area. But one important factor also that does not help the present Canadian climate is the situation that was created in Canada by the advent in Quebec, on November 15, 1976, of a Parti Quebecois government whose avowed objective, I repeat, is the separation of Quebec from the rest of the Canadian Confederation.
Even though we may be deluded or even taken in by the PQ ministers telling us that Quebec has lost nothing from an economic point of view since this event and that, according to the Minister of Industry, inquiries from interested investors are more numerous than ever in Quebec, we cannot be so sure when we talk to businessmen and industrialists. Their response indicates the opposite. These are simply attempts by the Parti Quebecois to appease the business community and the people of Quebec and to have them forget the cruel facts while the PQ government is busy introducing a whole series of measures for this campaign on the famous referendum, campaign which began on November 15, 1976. Whether we want it or not, whether we shut our eyes or keep them open, the situation in Quebec is reflected everywhere in Canada and in the edginess of foreign investors who would like to come here to improve their Canadian businesses.
What happened in Quebec last November may have been called an accident by some people, but I believe that it would not be realistic or even honest for any Canadian who knows the history of his country or has ever read it to forget that the problem facing our two founding races, French and English, did not start on November 15, 1976. It has existed since Confederation. However, it has become more acute at various stages of our history with the coming into the political arena of

French Canadians, great politicians, leaders inspired by a nationalism which is very healthy and necessary for the survival of the French element, not only in Quebec, but throughout Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I came to parliament as member for Bonaven-ture at the time when bombs were being placed in mailboxes in Montreal and under monuments in Quebec city, and so on. I for one have stated again and again to people all across Canada during the centennial year that what Quebec really wanted, was not to be given a special treatment, but to gain recognition of the identity, the language and the culture, of its French majority.
If since Confederation and in the course of these various difficult moments of our country's history all our Englishspeaking compatriots had shown more good will towards and less contempt for those "Catholic French Canadians, those French Canadian Pea Soups", outside as well as within Quebec, if they had understood as fortunately they seem to be doing today, our situation, we would not have had to use for so many years, and now in particular, we would not have had to use and waste our energy, our talent, our time and our money in the difficult economic situation we now know, discussing linguistic questions and constitutional changes. Mr. Speaker, I believe that all federal governments since 1962 have made fantastic efforts which no previous governments had ever made to give Francophones equality in their relations with federal institutions. When one considers the fierce opposition which all measures proposed in that area have met with in this the last half of the 20th century, in 1970-77, in some English-speaking areas, while the unity of our country was at stake, we should not, Mr. Speaker, be overly surprised with what happened in Quebec.
Was November 15, 1976, really necessary to finally get our compatriots or some of our English-speaking compatriots to see the light? What price, Mr. Speaker? I suggest it could have been avoided. But it seems that for some bold ones, you must be near catastrophe before starting to react in the face of danger. Let us still thank providence for even this late conversion of our compatriots or of some of them, and that conversion lets us foresee with confidence a solution to this problem which unfortunately has always divided us.
Quebeckers are federalists, Mr. Speaker. The Quebec people do not want to be isolated on this immense continent. They want to remain Canadians but they want to be full fledged citizens, respected everywhere in Canada, just as they have themselves always respected other Canadians. They want to take part in the great decisions which will affect their daily lives, their own and their children's future. They along with their countrymen want to keep developing this vast country so well endowed with natural wealth, and a great variety of regions which they and other Canadians are so proud and other nations so envious of. They are proud of their peaceful and free homeland which has been built thanks to the sacrifice and hard work of their fathers and ancestors.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a remarkable paragraph from her Majesty's Speech from the Throne:
October 25, 1977

Few countries are as blessed as Canada, where a wealth of freedom and of this world's goods is apparent for all to see. Perhaps only those who have come here from less fortunate lands can appreciate to the full the great good fortune of living in a country so favored by nature, and so enriched by its cultural diversity.

May I begin in the traditional way? 1 should like to congratulate the hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to Her Majesty's Speech from the Throne. I do not think there is anything I can say about their contributions except to sum them up in one word-and that word is "envy". I thought they did extraordinarily well. In all the years I have been here I never cease to marvel about the members who come into this House and, for the first time, are chosen to address a group of people who, by and large, are strangers, and make some sense out of what they do and put feeling and passion into their expressions of belief in being a Canadian. It was just a thrill for me to listen to those men doing that. They achieved at the very top level of this special craft.
While I am on this congratulatory kick I look toward Your Honour as you preside over our proceedings, the member of parliament for London East (Mr. Turner), a long-time friend and the Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole. And I think of your assistant, the hon. member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Ethier), and I wish you both well in the duties you carry out. This is a pre-election session and life is not always going to be easy for you; you will not always be looking down and seeing some mild fellow from Halifax-East Hants addressing you. You will be seeing some angry natives around here some night, probably late at night, making your life a little more difficult. In any event, whatever happens this session, we esteem you and we esteem your own particular deputy in the House and know that you will serve us well.

speechtext:
But we should be portraying more the nature of ourselves as an institution instead of the nature of what people try to pretend we are, whether we ourselves, going on the hustings, or the reporters in the press gallery who are so quick to have second opinions about us. In any event, the television age is here and we all have to live with it. We have to make a presentation of our handling of the public affairs of this nation we call Canada as best we can and I know that every last one of us, when we go home for this weekend with the whole bloom of the week upon us will learn very much from our constituents.
I want to touch on three or four topics tonight in the time which is given to me. One of them arises out of the personal and special interest 1 have as a chairman of a committee in which we have to deal in a special way with the meeting of government and the public. I refer to the Statutory Instruments Committee or perhaps I should say the Regulations Committee-that would probably make more sense to those who are listening to me-dealing with the orders in council

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. McCleave
and the proliferation of documents from ministers, departments, the cabinet and the like which do touch us all very much. The aspect 1 would like to talk about tonight does not deal with all that, but rather with the special case of where a person meets government through a form that has to be filled out to satisfy somebody in a government department. The forms I would like to consider tonight are two.
First of all, there are those which are being presented by the Public Service Commission of Canada to those who are graduating from higher institutions of learning. These are called post-secondary recruitment programs and I have such a form here. By and large I consider it a fair form, with one exception. When one is asked to go into such detail as one's academic achievements or what one has gone through by way of academic studies, notation 17 on this particular form not only asks you for your course number and title, but for the total number of hours per course, the number of credits, the length of the course, and whether it is a half course or a full course.
It seems to me that for someone who has gone through four years of university, for example, to be asked to retrace one's steps through that particular process and try to recall to the exact hour or half hour how much one has done, is going a little too far. These are young people. They may have been gifted when they went through their academic career and that part may have been duck soup to them. They made good marks, met every whim of their professor and wrote brilliant exams. Then suddenly they are thrust into that miserable old thing called the workaday world and perhaps another equally miserable thing known as an employer, one such being the Public Service Commission of Canada.
It strikes me we may be a society which depends too much on forms. You can take a person's social insurance number, take all sorts of other details from them and then give them a mark, A, B, C, or D, and punch it through a computer, but not necessarily come up with anything very meaningful. An absolute dunce might be able to answer these questions completely satisfactorily and be rated very highly, whereas a natural genius might not. I am not sure that Albert Einstein himself in his palmy days would have succeeded too well with this particular form. For one thing he was too diffident, but it is the Albert Einstein that we would like to get rather than some other type.
In any event, I think what is lacking here is a humanistic approach. It is not a question of how well one can fill in a form; it is a question of meeting with a prospective employer, talking with that person and outfolding one's personality in that way. I hope the Public Service Commission of Canada and my old friend, Mr. Edgar Gallant, who is the chairman and the only person in Canada whom I have heard speak English with an Oxford accent and French with a Parisian accent-hon. members can gather how gifted he is-will take these words of mine to heart.
On page 1 I am really surprised to see about one sixteenth of the page-a heck of a lot of space anyway-to decide this

momentous question: "D. Sex (for statistical purposes); Sexe (pour fins de stastiques)". Then there is a space for masculine or feminine, male or female. They give you all that space to make up your mind. I would have thought that about one tenth of the space provided would have sufficed and that the rest of the space might have been used to deal with one's other extraordinary abilities.
Another form I looked at-I searched for it today but it was lost among the other forms in my office-is one dealing with requests for financial assistance from the Department of Fisheries. I hope my hon. friend, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), will look at those forms and that the opposition fisheries critic will nod his head in agreement. He does, but he has not heard my question. That is comradeship and partnership.
What bugs me about the forms that you fill in for the Department of Fisheries is that you almost need a chartered accountant to assist you. Many of these people were not educated beyond the Grade 5 or 6 level. Good fishermen they are; statisticians and fillers-in of forms they are not. I suspect a large number of them miss thousands and thousands of dollars a year to which they are entitled under government programs simply became they do not have the patience or understanding to fill in those particular forms. Since I do not have the form in question here this evening, and I really cannot make my case without it, what I will do is guarantee that I will send the minister a letter containing my views.
I now turn to a national issue, but not one which is going to put any of my colleagues on either side of the House in trepidation in regard to their own brilliant positions as ministers or members of the opposition. What I want to talk about is the need, in my opinion, for a very important program to be carried on for those who are inmates in Canadian penitentiaries. I refer to a legal aid program. These people may be entitled to ask for legal advice and receive it with the state giving them some kind of help.
The reason I raise this matter is that there has been all kinds of correspondence back and forth on this matter between the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox), the chairman of the justice and legal affairs committee, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), and others, but somehow the message has not been as strong as it should be.
In my own area of the world, Atlantic Canada, a survey was conducted by the law and social problems class at Dalhousie Law School in 1972. This survey asked inmates of the penitentiaries at Dorchester, New Brunswick and Springhill, Nova Scotia, to identify the legal problems they experienced and how best their needs could be met. Of all the inmates they checked with, some 56.5 per cent had met some legal problem since they entered the penitentiary. But more important than that, 95.7 per cent had no financial means with which they could pay for the services of a lawyer. Their problems were in the area of family law, criminal law, and correctional law. The correctional law referred mainly to debtor-creditor relations or
October 25, 1977

problems. The survey also showed they had rather a hard time in reaching a lawyer.
There is one law firm of which Miss Deborah Gass is a member, called "Penitentiary Legal Services", established in Sackville, New Brunswick. I asked her if they did not get help from the spending estimates which were presented in February by the federal government, would that program be down the drain? At least the people engaged in the program would have to scratch around and do most of their work on other aspects of the law where they had clients who could pay, and then hope that they would be able to give some service to penitentiary inmates. When 1 asked her what it was she wanted, she wrote this to me:
What we suggest is that we be contracted to the federal government or the federal and provincial governments under a cost-share agreement similar to that under which provincial legal aid schemes operate. Services to the institutions is a full-time job and is somewhat specialized, in that most lawyers have little if any familiarity with correctional law.
As a lawyer, I would say "Guilty, Miss Gass; you have described me exactly and, I am sure, most of us in the House of Commons". But while we do not have that familiarity, at least our hearts can be in the right place.
Anyway, she took her case to me and to others and had a meeting with the Minister of Fisheries and several of his adornments on the other side, such as the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), and the member of the other place, Senator Margaret Norrie.
She responded positively to us by promising to look into the matter and see what could be done. Since I have put it on record, I know my friends on the other side will also add their very, very strong words.
I asked Miss Gass to do one thing before I took part in the throne speech debate and made this particular plea on behalf of legal services for those in penitentiaries. I asked her to provide me with some illustrations of what they were doing. She sent along 15 cases. I cannot refer to them all now because my time will be running out shortly, but I should like to mention as many typical cases as I can.
I will refer to seven out of the 15 illustrations which were sent to me. The first is the case of a young inmate, age 17, who has been diagnosed as mildly retarded. He was guilty of three car thefts, and the question was if that person should go to jail.
The second one was an inmate being transferred from a federal penitentiary in Dorchester to one in western Canada. He had a valuable ring which was taken from him before he left, so he said. He is trying to get the ring back.
The third one is an inmate who was severely beaten and attacked by another inmate in the prison gym during a movie. It was a fight for compensation under the Innocent Victims Crime Act, and the inmate was rewarded $1,500.
The fourth one is an inmate who had outstanding debts totalling approximately $10,000. He had no assets, and requested assistance in applying for the bankruptcy services of
The Address-Mr. McCleave
the federal trustee. Anybody who says that inmates are free to choose their lawyers like anybody else is wrong. They are in jail and they have no means of earning incomes. They have no money-crime does not pay after all-and then they are being asked to hire outside lawyers, which is impossible. I hope the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General will take this to heart.
The fifth case involves an inmate's father who died suddenly and had named no beneficiary in his insurance policy. The inmate, being the legal heir, sought help to settle the estate.
The sixth case is that of an inmate's mother who wished a divorce. She was on welfare and could not afford the services of a lawyer. Therefore the inmate requested legal assistance for his mother.
The seventh case is that of an inmate who sold his truck but was still owed $110 on it. That might not seem like much to anyone here tonight, but to that person it meant that it was the end of the world. He attempted to contact the debtor on several occasions but received no reply. However, the legal services group sent a letter to the debtor and the debt was acknowledged after a little bit of a fight. A settlement of $55 was negotiated, so the inmate was ahead by that much. The foregoing are some samples of what these people are up against.
If anyone in this Chamber tried to establish a successful law practice with those types of cases, I am sure he would be reduced to living on the parish as well. These people have very human problems. It is a matter of rehabilitating them and returning them to society as useful people. I hope their pleas to myself and others succeed.
In order to follow this up a little bit more, since I promised to spend a larger part of my speech on this subject than any other topic, I would suggest through Your Honour to the Bars of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick that being a lawyer is not easy because of the fees and insurance which have to be paid. Someone located in Sackville, New Brunswick, or across the border in Amherst, Nova Scotia, who primarily services the inmates of penitentiaries and other federal institutions, will not come home with any real harvest even if he has received help from the federal treasury. I hope the Bars of those two provinces, which have been very, very co-operative so far, would recognize that there should be some special type of law firm established in that isthmus between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. 1 am not saying that one has to be a member of the Nova Scotia Bar and not a member of the New Brunswick Bar. The hon. member for Gloucester is nodding his head. I am sure he understands what I am getting at. There must be allowances made for the special circumstances these hot, storefront lawyers are going into when they try to help people.
The name of our particular game in this parliament is jobs. How well we do that and how well we come through the current hardships afflicting the country will make or break a lot of hon. members in this Chamber. I do not think the public expect miracles from us, but they do expect an effort from us. My own philosophy is that I do not believe we can spend our

October 25, 1977
The Address-Mr. McCleave
way to prosperity. We have tried that, and we are approximately $8 billion in the hole this year.

The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) is referring to $9.2 billion. Because he is more knowledgeable about those figures than I am, he is probably correct. This is a substantial cry from the approximate $7 billion forecast with which we started this fiscal year. We thought the country would go in the hole by that amount. We have proven to ourselves that we cannot spend our way to prosperity. Therefore, whatever initiatives are left to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien)-God knows I feel for the man and I will feel for his successor as well-they will be restricted and will depend on imagination, effort, and some old and ancient concepts which are being rediscovered, such as incentives, good hard elbow grease, and "let the state stay away, we will try to solve it on our own."
The only areas where federal spending can work are areas where federal spending has an obligation to work. For example, we have an obligation to the Department of National Defence. Ships, tanks, airplanes and various other things have to be built. They can be built in certain areas which have shipyards, aircraft plants, or the tank plants. One could use those to buttress the employment there. These things have to be bought. Heaven only knows the requirements of the navy have been put off for a long period of time. Sooner or later the government has to face the fact that these things have to be bought.
There is an absolute necessity for the government to create incentives and to take special tax measures. We will have an opportunity when the Bank Act comes up to see what we can do for small business, and that is important. We will not lose our shirts if we try to devise measures in this parliament which will help the tens of thousands of small businesses across this country to create more jobs.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the October 17, 1977, edition of the London Free Press, which reads as follows:
One intriguing new idea has been the proposal by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business that special tax credits be given to firms that increase their employment; it would have its greatest impact on small firms in labour-intensive business. It is these firms which suffer the most from high minimum wages and from their need to match Canada Pension Plan and unemployment deductions, and to pay other fringe benefits-and from the high cost of meeting the myriad requests of government for reports.
That makes an awful lot of sense to me. I should like to conclude by saying two things. One I will say now, the other I will say at a later time. There will be another debate, they always come around. They are like taxis in New York.
What I want to say is that in times of difficulty it is not only for each of us to think of answers but for each of us to provide those answers as best we can. I have not touched on the social problem that is besetting our nation-the future of Canada. I have touched on other matters and I have mentioned briefly

the economic one, but if I had anything to guide me over this particular winter of difficulty, there would be two things: one would be to think Canadian, and the other would be to buy Canadian. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to congratulate the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and of course, my colleague from the Mari-times, the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood). They have both made excellent contributions to the House.

1 might say that when the hon. member for Malpeque was describing his constituency in such a poetic way I thought for a moment that he was speaking about my constituency. In fact, many people do not realize that both my constituency and his are as similar as are other constituencies in Canada, despite the fact that they are in different provinces.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we are now going through difficult times not only in economic but also in politic terms. For the first time in the history of this country, a provincial government wishes to bring about a complete change in the political structures of that province within the Canadian Confederation. As a member of the French-speaking minority outside Quebec, I am most concerned with this matter.
As a matter of fact, all Acadians have been very concerned with the Canadian situation for the past year or so. They are worried because in the past they have benefitted from the fact that Quebec belonged to the Confederation. It would be almost impossible and unthinkable for us, the Acadians who are living in the Maritime provinces, to expect that Canada would make linguistic and cultural concessions to us if it were not for the province of Quebec. The fact that that province which we very much admire and have always been proud of is considering a totally new role within the Canadian Confederation is of great concern to us. Of course, the stand by the Quebec Premier, Mr. Levesque, and his party, advocating independence or sovereignty within an economic association with the rest of Canada, simply means that Quebec considers itself as the only voice of French-speaking Canadians.
The problem of Quebec nationalism is not a new one and we are concerned that the Parti Quebecois put foward such an idea because this concept of Quebec nationalism seems to mean that they will negotiate another arrangement with the other nine provinces on behalf of all French-speaking Canadians. At that time, some concessions will be necessary. Whether we think of a sovereignty-association or a renewed Federalism or any other special status, some constitutional concessions will eventually have to be made to Quebec for the sake of the French-speaking group.
Then the minorities outside Quebec could not claim anything and it would be difficult for them to get concessions as
October 25, 1977

they do today, among other things for instance to work in their own language in the federal public service or the fact that, just as Quebecers, Francophones outside Quebec have legal rights to services in their own language. All those advantages could be lost if Quebec were to quit Confederation.
Mr. Speaker, we often hear, specially from members opposite, that this government lays too much emphasis on the national unity issue, that we have more serious economic problems which need our attention. In the same breath those people claim that we have had problems over national unity ever since the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. I believe they mislead themselves if they think that. For many years some regions in Canada have identified themselves on a regional basis, and that may be normal as we have a huge country and a scattered population. So we have more public administration per capita than in other countries.
Therefore regions and people give much importance to their own area; we see in the Maritimes, in the Prairies, in western Canada and in Quebec where it is demonstrated in another way. It all revolves around culture and language. But national tension in this country is nothing new and you do not know the situation if you say that the approach of this government, of this Prime Minister, which created that issue. Indeed, as I said earlier, the nationalist movement in Quebec dates from way back and as you know, Mr. Speaker, because you are from that province, that issue and that concept are not new.
Nowadays, in fact, they are simply expressed in another way, by another group, by another political party and by some people who choose another way even though they have the same idea. Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk briefly about my riding, my own area in Canada. I stated earlier that most Acadians, indeed all Acadians, are much concerned by the present situation in Canada and also by the political situation in their own province.
Acadians in New Brunswick have made tremendous progress since the sixties because they succeeded in finding allies among others, in other areas of the province, because they have been willing to accept political arrangements, structural changes, although they were not constitutional structures; they have adopted new political arrangements which gave them the opportunity to restructure their community, to improve their standard of living, but also gave them opportunities on the linguistic side, a legislation on official languages. The Official Languages Act of New Brunswick is very important to us, even though it has some weaknesses and is not perhaps as important from the administrative support point of view as Canada's Official Languages Act. But obviously Acadians, specially those who live in northeastern New Brunswick, are preoccupied by the economic situation. The issue of national unity looms larger than the economic one. We must deal with both.
Playing down the importance of the problem between the two founding peoples of Canada will get us nowhere. Indeed, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) made it quite clear yesterday that when tackling both problems and trying to put one ahead of the other, we are mistaken
The Address-Mr. Breau
because if no solution is found to the national unity problem in Canada, the international business community outside this country will always feel some uncertainty about its future, which will affect investments here and our ability to secure markets abroad.
To revert to the economic situation in my riding, in addition to setting up national programs such as those in the social area, health insurance, unemployment insurance, sharp increase in old age pensions, and family allowances, the government has helped out low income areas. Furthermore, since 1966 the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been involved in special agreements aimed at raising the standard of living and improving the economic structures of northeastern New Brunswick. Between 1966 and 1976 we have benefited from one of the first FRED agreements-the Fund for Rural Economic Development-which is a federal-provincial agreement designed to define certain problems by analyzing them and proposing solutions. This agreement has led to some success but also disappointment in some other cases.
It is very difficult to stimulate development in an area such as ours because as soon as you start defining a problem or identifying it, it is normal that the psychological response from the people living in the area be negative from the outset since people are likely to put the blame on governments or systems which have tolerated the kind of situation in which they have lived for so long. Consequently many hopes entertained by people of our region have been met with disappointment because, when these agreements were announced, they expected that development would be easier than it actually turned out to be. Anyway, the ten-year agreement of 1966 to 1976 has been replaced this summer by a new one signed by my colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) and the premier of New Brunswick. It changes slightly our approach toward development compared to the former type of agreement and we hope it will contribute a great deal more to improving the economic structure of that region.
This agreement provides outlays of more than $95 million within the next five years and is intented above all to create jobs and consequently enhance industrial development. Instead of coming up with social and community development or carrying out social experiments as contained in the former agreement, the new one will have a more industrially minded outlook. It seeks to develop major industrial centres which will attract investments and consequently create jobs. Naturally this agreement must be considered within the framework of other DREE programs such as the road agreement which greatly benefits northeastern New Brunswick and which, we hope, will help in rebuilding a major segment of Highways 11, 17 and 8.
Naturally, the other federal government departments will also have to keep up their good work in the field of transportation, in the field of maritime and marine structures, because the fisheries are very important in that region, and also in many other fields. We have heard a lot lately about the problems affecting the mining sector.

October 25, 1977
The Address

Mr. Breau
There is in my riding an important mining industry, and there are several others in the area, but particularly the most important mining industry in my riding, the Brunswick Mining and Smelting, is also having difficulties because world markets are depressed. And of course, unless that situation improves, many other efforts the government will try to make through the DREE agreement will not meet with the expected success.
Anyway, we are moderately optimistic that the federal government investment will help improve the economic structure of northeastern New Brunswick to the point that our area could become a lot more self sufficient than it has been in the past. But of course, the other economically oriented departments, as I said, will also have to keep on not only planning but investing in that area. And of course, the Canadian economy will have to remain strong, the federal government will also have to carry on its efforts to redistribute wealth in this country if people in that area are really to see a considerable change.
I should like to deal briefly with the debate on the economy now being carried on. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) made a very important statement on this.
There is high unemployment in my constituency and it is chronic in that it is bad this year and expected to be worse next year because of restraints in provincial and federal government spending, and also because investment is low. I meet more and more unemployed tradespeople now than ever before. This chronic unemployment problem is due mainly to restraints in spending and less investment by the private sector.
An important aspect of the economy of New Brunswick in the last ten or 15 years has been the construction of major projects in the energy field and some other areas, which have created a lot of economic activity and employment. Tradespeople earn high salaries and this creates an economic spinoff in the whole province, but this has not been evident in the last year and it is not expected any projects will get off the ground in the months to come.
I hope economic restraints can be lifted before too long as the Atlantic economy has suffered more than other parts of the country from their effects. I find the position of the opposition very contradictory when they speak of less intervention in the economy, less spending by government, less deficits-

I am glad the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) emphasizes what I am saying. I wish he could reconcile it with what he said last Thursday evening when he condemned the Minister of Finance for not having done anything. I should like him to explain how he expects the economy to pick up if there is not more government spending in the Atlantic provinces. His colleagues from there always bring pressure for more government spending.

In the month of September my colleagues from the Atlantic provinces and I went around the area and listened to what a lot of community leaders and business leaders had to say. The thing foremost on their minds is the improvement of economic structures, improvement in the standard of living, more investment by government, more spending and more intervention by government.
The Tory party is advocating less government intervention and less government spending, but let us not be fooled by that. They are advocating a system of laissez-faire whereby the private sector will determine where it wants to go. That, of course, would benefit central Canada because that is where most of the industry of this country is located. However, if we want to maintain an equal standard of living and equal opportunities, the government has to intervene in the economy and has to take money from taxpayers and spend to initiate projects and programs across the country so that people across the country can have equal opportunities for finding decent jobs.

Despite the fact that we have a relatively good record of creating employment in Canada and in the Atlantic provinces, we need to create more, for the simple reason that many young people and more and more women are entering the labour force.

Many people get upset about deficits, justifiably, I suppose. Because the opposition is in the game of politics, it exaggerates the effects of deficits. The reason we have deficits is not that spending has gone wild; it is strictly because there has been an economic slowdown in the world and in Canada. There is less industrial activity, and therefore a smaller amount of corporate tax is being collected. Less revenue is coming in because of the economic slowdown in the western world including this country, and therefore we have a deficit.
Hon. members opposite are saying that we should slash the deficit right away and that it is terrible, because they are interested only in making political points. There are only two ways to slash deficits, either by increasing taxes or by reducing government spending drastically. If we do the latter, the five eastern provinces, and probably Manitoba, would suffer. The other regions of the country would probably be able to get by pretty well.
It is not difficult right now for the Government of Canada to manage its debt and its deficit. The latest issue of Canada Savings Bonds was sold in record time, for the simple reason that people are saving money. I say it is not so bad, at a time of economic slowdown, for the government to have some

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE IN CASE OF MR. SANT SINGH

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE IN CASE OF MR. SANT SINGH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 20 I raised a question with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) with regard to a public servant who had been employed in that department since 1967. That public servant is Mr. Sant Singh. He was classified as an ES2 on January 1, 1970. He was and is a member of the bargaining unit represented by the Economists, Sociologists and Statisticians Association, and was covered by a collective agreement.
This question has worried me very much because of its implications for the Public Service of Canada. It is a fact that he had risen in the public service to the fifth salary rate and he had been promoted in terms of his salary in any event to the sixth salary rate. In fact he was receiving a salary at that rate.
In terms of salary, he had crossed the "barrier," as it is known in the public service. That requires approval of the deputy minister or deputy head of the department. He was then informed that, for some reason or other, the department had made a mistake and they were paying him too highly. It was not his mistake. It was a mistake of the department.
In accordance with the standard rules, he was sent for a performance assessment. It is interesting to note that this public servant had two of them. On his assessment, his superior was called, a person who knew him very well. This was his assessment, and I quote:
I am very pleased to recommend that this Departmental Performance Assessment Committee approve the movement of Mr. Sant P. Singh beyond the barrier in the ES-2 scale of rates. Mr. Singh has been a member of my staff since February 24, 1969, and has been classified as ES-2 since January 1, 1970. I have been highly satisfied and pleased with his performance, competence, initiative, and loyalty-
The deputy minister, without interviewing the man, said he was not satisfied with that and sent him back for a second assessment. In the course of this unhappy period, the second assessment was held. Mr. Arthur Smith, his immediate supervisor, was not present on that occasion.
In the meantime, some question had been raised about the fact that Mr. Sant Singh had run in the constituency of Pontiac as a Conservative candidate against the sitting member for Pontiac (Mr. Lefebvre). His judgment was questioned by Mr. Mennie, a member of the department. In fact the evidence was that this had a great bearing on the outcome of the case.
The upshot of it is that he was not approved and he aggrieved. What did Mr. O'Shea, the grievance officer find? First, he found that none of the reports he was entitled to see under the policy of the department would be shown to him.
Second, he found as a fact that the political involvement of this public servant, with consent under the normal rules, had affected the mind of the deputy minister, and that ought not to have been the case.
Third, he found that there had been some hanky-panky in terms of the two different boards, the first assessment board

with one set of witnesses and the other with another set of witnesses. Therefore the evidence was stacked against him.
I asked the minister whether she would intervene to launch an appeal against the appeal that had been launched by the department so that they would withdraw their appeal. Her answer was of course that they do not interfere with the judicial process. All that has happened is that the appeal has been launched. There has been no hearing by the judge.
This case cries out for action by the minister as head of the department. It is her responsibility to intervene for the welfare of her public servants. She has refused to do that. I charge her with dereliction of her duty.
I hope that when the parliamentary secretary rises in his place tonight he will indicate that he has decided to enter this matter and will ask the solicitor of the department to withdraw the notice of appeal so that this public servant, who has been found to be a man of initiative, competence, loyalty, and all the other adjectives which apply to him, can be granted that to which he is entitled, according to the finding of the adjudicator.
This is not surmise. It is not instinct. The cause I plead on behalf of Sant Singh and of all public servants who are caught in this process of hiring and firing in the public service is based on an adjudication. There is no justification whatsoever for Mr. Sant Singh to be penalized, either for his political involvement or anything else. I think the government owes the adjudicator at least the courtesy of withdrawing this appeal, and I ask the parliamentary secretary to relieve Mr. Singh from the burden he bears as a result of the failure of his minister to look to her constitutional duties with respect to public servants.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE IN CASE OF MR. SANT SINGH
speechtext:
The minister has stated that she does not intend to interfere in any way with the process established by regulations concerning the behaviour, classification and promotion of civil servants, and it would seem that the answer given at that time might have been sufficient for the hon. member. Nevertheless, I propose to go further.
This case revolves around an interpretation of a section of the collective agreement entered into by the employee's union and his employer, the Government of Canada. The collective agreement is with the Economics, Sociology and Statistics
October 25, 1977

Group (ES) and contains a section whereby employees at levels three and five can have their pay increased, or their progression in the pay range accelerated, by progressing beyond the so-called "barrier". Progression beyond the "barrier" is based upon the work performance of the employee. A departmental assessment committee reviews the work performance of the employee and, if that performance in the judgment of the committee meets the necessary criteria, a favourable recommendation is made and forwarded to the deputy minister for approval. If the deputy minister agrees with the performance assessment committee's recommendation, the employee's pay is adjusted to the first step beyond the "barrier". Such progression in the pay range is commonly called "progression beyond the barrier".
It is very important to note, however, that progression beyond the so-called barrier is not a promotion in the sense that the employee has moved up a level in his occupational group. I believe the hon. member told us that really what had happened was that he was given an increase in pay and there was no suggestion he was going to a different level of employment. No appointment is involved; the matter is only a question of pay administration.
The departmental assessment committee which reviewed Mr. Singh's performance in early 1976 issued a report that had conflicting recommendations and contained little supporting evidence in favour of the recommendation that the employee proceed beyond the ES-5 "barrier". The report of a second committee was invalid because of a technical flaw. For these reasons, the deputy minister did not give his approval to the performance assessment committee's report. Because the deputy minister's approval is required by the collective agreement, the employee's pay could not be raised.
Mr. Singh presented a grievance to the department over the fact that he had not been placed above the ES-5 barrier. When this was denied, he referred the grievance to adjudication. At the hearing before the adjudicator, the grievor alleged the collective agreement had not been properly applied with respect to his pay. The employer claimed that progression beyond the ES-5 barrier requires the formal approval of the deputy minister, but because that approval has not been given, the employee cannot proceed beyond the so-called barrier in the ES-5 pay scale.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF FLUORSPAR MINE AT ST. LAWRENCE, NEWFOUNDLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF FLUORSPAR MINE AT ST. LAWRENCE, NEWFOUNDLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with a question I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on October 20 about a
Adjournment Debate
community which has been sentenced to death by Alcan Limited. This is the community of St. Lawrence, Newfoundland, where a fluorspar mine had been operating since the 1930's. Alcan announced earlier this spring that they were going to close this fluorspar mine, which is the only operating fluorspar mine in Canada.
Alcan still need fluorspar but they are now going to get their fluorspar from Mexico, where they have discovered that, as a result of cheap Mexican labour, they can import fluorspar from Mexico at less cost to themselves than operating the mine they own in St. Lawrence.
To add to the gravity of the situation, the people of St. Lawrence who have worked in the fluorspar mine have had a very tragic history. They worked for at least 30 years suffering unknowingly from radiation as a result of radon gas in the environment, emanating from the fluorspar mine. During the 1930's and 1940's they worked in the most primitive of conditions. The result was that several hundred of these people, a very high proportion of the work force, developed cancer. In the old days this cancer was said not to be related to their working conditions, and for years their widows or dependants did not receive any adequate or any workmen's compensation. This was eventually cleared up in the 1950's when a link was established between their working conditions and the cancer from which they died. In any event, there are books which have been written about this very tragic situation.
Alcan have discovered that they can now import their fluorspar from Mexico more cheaply than they can mine it in St. Lawrence, so they have decided to shut the mine and to lay-off the 400 workers employed there.
There is very little that the government of Newfoundland can do about this. The government of Newfoundland could seize their assets in Newfoundland, but they would be seizing assets which this company has already decided to abandon. The Newfoundland government therefore has no muscle to use on this group of callous employers. The government of Newfoundland is doing some studies to see whether there is an alternate mining operation which somebody else might be persuaded to take on. It is also looking to see whether a fresh fish filleting plant could be established there to provide employment. So the government of Newfoundland is doing what it can.
On July 21 it formally asked the then minister of industry, trade and commerce in a letter from the minister of intergovernmental affairs of Newfoundland whether the Canadian government would impose a tariff on the importation of fluorspar into Canada or impose quotas on fluorspar imported into Canada in order to put some pressure on Alcan to continue the operation of this mine. It was a simple request. No tariff has been imposed on fluorspar until now. It is the only way this decision might be reversed. The Government of Canada did not reply to the letter which was sent three months ago, until an answer was received on October 21 from the minister.

October 25, 1977
Adjournment Debate
I raised a question in the House on October 20, and the present minister did not answer the real question. He indicated that the federal government is making an effort to work out an assessment of the possibility of restoring the mine in order for it to become a viable operation in the future. That is gob-bledygook. That was not an answer from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) to the government of Newfoundland.
A second letter was written on October 11, 1977, and that is the letter to which the present minister is responding. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) has abandoned his 400 constituents. He did not put any pressure on the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, nor on the Government of Canada, to impose a tariff or to impose a quota.
Are we to close down all our industries in Canada? Are we to find Chinese coolies, poor Mexican peasants or whoever, to mine ore more cheaply than we can? Are we to forget the history of the poor miners at St. Lawrence? Are we to abandon them? If there is a lay-off in Ontario, the newspapers are full of it. We have seen the coverage of the recent INCO situation. If it is in Newfoundland, out of sight and out of mind, it is forgotten. That is one of the complaints of eastern Canada. Our people are thrown in the dustbin and forgotten. Therefore 1 object to the Minister's answer which he gave the other day. He indicated that he would reply soon. I also object to the letter he sent down, because it is a nothing letter.
1 ask the minister, through his parliamentary secretary, to have the Government of Canada take some action or explain to this House and the people of Canada what it is doing to protect these people. They have been abandoned by Alcan, which is a multinational corporation. It has no conscience, and these people were abandoned without a twinge of regret. After years of toil, hundreds of men are being deserted, as well as widows and children who are on pensions because of the previous terrible conditions that existed in the fluorspar mines.
In 1975 when I was the provincial minister of mines and energy, I visited the mines. If the mines are abandoned as they are now, they will begin to flood. If the minister does not take action soon, it will be too late. The miners are being laid off now, and the final abandonment will occur in February of 1978. That was postponed because of assistance received from the government of Newfoundland, not the Government of Canada. The minister has little time left, because they are no longer operating several of the shafts. They are starting to flood. People are being laid off now.
Action is needed. If there is no action, then surely the federal government owes an explanation to the people of St. Lawrence of why it cannot take some action to assist them. Are they to be put on the dole because Alcan can buy fluorspar from Mexico? Mexico is a country which pays much lower wages and has much more primitive working conditions than the miners now have at St. Lawrence after 50 years of effort by their union and by themselves to improve their lot.

The minister should be made aware of the fact that his answer is most unsatisfactory. The Newfoundland minister of intergovernmental affairs gave a press conference today to outline to the people of Newfoundland the abandonment by the federal government of its responsibilities to these people. I ask the parliamentary secretary to pass on to his minister the request that some action be taken soon, or confirm the death knell.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-MINING REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO IMPROVE ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
INDUSTRY-MINING REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO IMPROVE ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday, October 19, I raised in this House a question with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) regarding the fact that Falconbridge had announced a lay-off of some 500 workers to take effect by the end of December, 1977. I also raised with the minister at that time the fact that rumours were floating around the Sudbury basin with respect to the INCO lay-offs.
The minister replied in a typical manner, that is, he gave me a non-answer to the effect that he was aware of soft markets and he was exploring possibilities of finding solutions to these problems. But as long ago as April 17, 1973, as reported on
October 25, 1977

page 3370 of Hansard, I raised the question with the then minister of manpower and immigration:
Has the minister obtained from International Nickel Company projected employment and production levels at this company over the next few years? If not, is it the minister's intention to ask INCO to provide his Manpower consultative services with such information?
The minister's response in 1973 was to the effect that INCO was not required by law to consult with his department, but that:
the department encourages employers to inform us as early as possible of any decisions that will cause significant employment shifts, expansions and dislocations.
Then there is this gem of a statement in the minister's letter to me, dated April 18, 1973, which reads as follows:
Departmental officers enjoy a good working relationship with INCO, as indeed with corporations in all industrial sectors.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is with incredulity that I heard in the House last Friday, October 21, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) say in answer to a question from a member of the opposition, as reported on page 115 of Hansard:
Second, 1 met with two members from International Nickel who spelled out for us, the night before the announcement, the action they proposed to take.
It is fairly obvious that the government's view of a good working relationship with INCO and INCO's view of such a relationship comprise a phone call the night before a major announcement about a lay-off is made. Needless to say, this government's relationship with Falconbridge Nickel Mines is just as close as its relationship with INCO.
But INCO not only treats the government in an off-hand and cavalier fashion. It even treats its employees' representatives in an off-hand, callous, and lying fashion, because on September 23 of this year, at a meeting held among officials of the INCO, Mr. Woodley and Mr. Kramer representing the company, and Mr. Moreau, Mr. Sammut, Mr. Robinson and Mr. Ayres representing the union of workers at Port Colborne, a meeting which took place at two o'clock in the afternoon, the following question was put to the company, whether they were prepared to consider shifting the Port Colborne workers who were laid off to the Sudbury and Thompson areas. The company replied:
That is correct. We will review the job situation in each of these areas before we would offer jobs at these locations. As we get closer to January, we will have a much better feel of the situation. At present there is no problem for jobs at Thompson. It is felt that by January 30th Sudbury will be in a hiring position.
Those are responsible officials of the International Nickel Company speaking to the workers' representatives at a meeting, and these are the minutes as printed by INCO of Canada.
It is painfully obvious that the government has failed miserably not only in planning the economy of Canada but, what is even more important, in keeping on top of major corporation development plans.
Even as INCO announced the 3,400-man layoff in Canada and we were demonstrating our protest to that announcement
Adjournment Debate
this past week end, a cargo ship, the S.S. Latija, docked in Vancouver from Japan and was unloaded on October 21, 22, and 23. And what was unloaded? Seven hundred boxes, each containing 2,600 pounds of nickel carbonate from Japan. This material, 1,820,000 pounds of nickel carbonate, was destined for the Sheritt Gordon Refinery, Fort Saskatchewan.
What is going on, Mr. Speaker? That is the stuff we produce in the Sudbury basin. We have heard ministers say that our low interest loans to INCO's subsidiaries in the Third World countries are assisting those countries. Why are we importing nickel carbonate from Japan when we produce it ourselves? Since when has Japan joined the Third World?
Today, in meetings between INCO officials, union leaders and provincial government ministers, Dr. Smith, an INCO economist who is also on the board of directors of the company, noted that Japan has very high import tariffs on processed nickel products. They encourage import matter only. It is fairly obvious that the Japanese government places a great deal of emphasis on keeping its industry labour intensive, while we continue to operate like some banana republic.
There is no question that the government has mismanaged Canada's economy. The only immediate response is to instruct INCO and Falconbridge to accept the unions' five-point program, as well as the establishment of a government stockpile of nickel, and to rescind the layoff order at INCO and Falconbridge.
The time has also come for a special parliamentary committee to be established to investigate the metals industry in Canada, and INCO's and Falconbridge's recent layoffs and cutback announcements in particular.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-MINING REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO IMPROVE ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announced layoff of some 2,200 people at Sudbury results from depressed market conditions for nickel throughout the world. After the layoffs take effect, INCO will continue to operate most of its Ontario facilities and will employ some 15,000 people in its Ontario division.
Since early 1975 INCO has been producing more nickel in Canada than it has been able to sell in world markets, and has accumulated a very large inventory of Finished nickel products. The excess production resulted in maintenance of employment at the company's Canadian facilities in anticipation of an upturn in world demand. The anticipated increase in demand has not materialized and is not expected in the near term.
A high level of inventories of nickel producers and excess output continue to exert a downward pressure on prices. In order to arrive at a better balance between supply and demand, a rate of production commensurate with consumption and a reduction of inventory are necessary.
In mid 1977 the company announced that it would reduce production at Sudbury and at Thompson by ceasing the hiring of replacements for employees leaving the company's work force.

October 25, 1977
Adjournment Debate
INCO has also announced it will reduce production at its operations in Indonesia and Guatemala to levels substantially below those planned for 1978-79. These operations are based on lateritic ore bodies as distinct from the sulphide deposits which INCO mines in Canada. Nickel output from laterites is expected to become increasingly important in the longer term because the reserves are much larger than Canadian reserves and laterites can be mined by open pit methods which require less labour than the underground mining operations in Canada.
Because of the lack of demand in world markets for most metals, it should be anticipated that adjustments in production rates will occur.
While international consultations amongst producers and consumers might make a contribution toward bringing about
an improvement in the market situation in the longer term, the government's immediate concern is to deal with the threatened lay off of workers in the Sudbury area. It is for this reason that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is meeting with the company and the union to consider implementation of the various programs under his direction.
I want to assure the hon. member that the government has the real and firm intention of going ahead with programs to help the people of Sudbury, and I do not think we can play politics with such a situation.
